item.title: The pink bus experience: A smoother ride, if you can catch it
item.description:
For hours, the pink bus was nowhere to be found.
At Farmgate, in front of the National Parliament building and near Dhanmondi Road 27, repeated attempts to catch Dhaka’s newly introduced women-only bus ended in disappointment.
There was no readily available timetable to indicate when it would arrive or where exactly passengers should wait.
The search eventually led to the Mohammadpur bus depot, where an official provided the crucial information: the bus leaves at 8:40am and makes its return journey from Motijheel around 5:15pm.
On Thursday, the search began again, this time with a destination and departure time in hand.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
At 8:25am, several red BRTC double-decker buses were already leaving the Mohammadpur depot. Further inside stood the much-sought-after pink bus.
From a distance, it appeared almost empty.
Three or four women were seated downstairs, with another five or six on the upper deck. The driver had yet to arrive.
Then Irin appeared, dressed in pink, ready to take the wheel of the double-decker.
After completing her checks, she started the engine. As the bus moved forward inside the depot, women began boarding. Within minutes, the once nearly empty vehicle was filling up.
At 8:40am, it finally set off towards Motijheel.
The journey took the bus through Shankar, Jigatala, City College, New Market, Nilkhet, Palashi, Shaheed Minar, Doel Chattar and the Secretariat before reaching Motijheel.
Near Chhayanaut in Shankar, several women waved for the bus to stop. About five climbed aboard, visibly relieved to have caught it.
Among them was Tamanna Khatun, an employee of Mercantile Bank who has used the service regularly since its introduction.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
She said she sometimes misses the bus by just a minute or two. On this morning, she was fortunate.
Her office closes at 5pm, allowing her to catch the return service when her schedule permits.
Further along the route, a woman travelling by rickshaw signalled for the bus. She initially struggled to board, prompting the driver to stop again.
Conductor Ayesha Siddiqui reminded her that attempting to board directly from a moving rickshaw was dangerous and advised her to get down safely before approaching the bus.
At City College, Tanzila, a Southeast Bank employee, joined the passengers.
For her, the service has made commuting considerably easier.
Previously dependent on ordinary local buses, she can now reach her office for just Tk20.
“The biggest advantage is that this bus is exclusively for women. Even if a seat isn’t available, standing doesn’t feel uncomfortable,” she said.
She particularly appreciated having women serving as both driver and conductor.
But her praise came with a reservation: the service operates only one round trip a day.
“If there were two more trips, it would be much more convenient,” she said.
On the upper deck, Lamia, a private-sector employee, described a similar problem.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
She has travelled along the Mohammadpur-Motijheel corridor since 2018 and said the bus had previously operated with male drivers before being refurbished and relaunched as the Pink Bus.
Her morning routine involves taking her child to school in Jigatala before boarding the bus for work.
But with only one morning departure, missing it means finding another way to reach the office.
She believes at least two morning services are necessary to make the initiative dependable.
As the bus reached Nilkhet, a few men attempted to board, apparently unaware that it was reserved for women. Female passengers informed them of the restriction.
Passengers began getting off at Shaheed Minar, Doel Chattar and the Secretariat. By Shapla Chattar, the bus was nearly empty.
At approximately 9:30am, it entered the Motijheel depot.
The morning journey had taken about 50 minutes.
At the depot, Irin finally had time to talk.
Before joining the Pink Bus service, she drove private cars. Handling a double-decker initially seemed daunting, particularly the unfamiliar stopping points and passenger boarding procedures.
“At first, I was uncertain about things like where to stop, what procedures to follow, and where passengers would board,” she said.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
“But over the last two months, everything has become quite simple.”
The sight of a woman driving a double-decker initially attracted considerable attention.
Some onlookers expressed surprise that women were now driving such large vehicles.
But Irin said her experience with fellow drivers had largely been positive.
Male drivers often make way for her, sometimes calling out, “Go ahead, ostad.”
Some have even offered her water during journeys.
“I don’t know about others, but I truly enjoy this profession,” she said.
The service has also created opportunities for women conductors such as Ayesha.
Yet the working arrangements present their own challenges.
Drivers and conductors serving routes from Mohammadpur, Mirpur, Jatrabari and Narayanganj arrive at the Motijheel depot around 9:30am and may have to wait until 5pm before their next departure.
Several drivers said rotating duties would allow them to spend more time with their families instead of remaining at the depot throughout the day.
Passenger numbers also reveal the limitations of the existing schedule.
According to conductor Ayesha, morning ticket sales frequently exceed Tk2,000, while afternoon collections range between Tk600 and Tk800.
Daily sales total approximately Tk3,000, she said.
The difference suggests stronger demand during the morning commute, while the afternoon departure does not suit many passengers’ working hours.
Ayesha said taking the alternative route through Shahbagh could attract another six or seven passengers.
For the women who use it, the Pink Bus represents a welcome change in everyday travel. The women-only environment, female crew and affordable fares offer a degree of comfort that passengers say is often missing from ordinary public transport.
But the journey also exposes a fundamental challenge.
A service designed to make commuting easier remains difficult to find, and a missed departure can mean waiting until the next day.
The pink bus has begun to earn the confidence of its passengers. Making it a dependable part of their daily lives will require more trips, accessible schedules and better coordination with the hours women actually travel.

item.title: Temple of the Golden Pavilion: Kyoto's iconic Zen sanctuary
item.description:
In early September of 2017, the weather in Kyoto was transitioning from the lingering heat of late summer to the subtle relief brought by early autumn breezes. Yet, as I stepped inside the grounds of one of Japan’s most iconic and photographed landmarks—Kinkaku-ji (the Temple of the Golden Pavilion)—the afternoon remained predominantly hot, sunny, and humid.
At first sight of this world-renowned Zen Buddhist temple in northern Kyoto, I was utterly awestruck. Its top two floors, completely covered in brilliant gold leaf, cast a flawless reflection onto the surrounding water. It is no wonder the Japanese call this body of water Kyōko-chi, which literally translates to "Mirror Pond".
Behind the visitors, Temple of the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji), is seen beautifully across the Mirror Pond (Kyoko-chi). Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
While that autumnal journey took me to many of Kyoto's sacred Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines, this UNESCO World Heritage Site remains an absolute favorite—not only for its breathtaking visual beauty, but also for its profound ambience of calm and its fascinating historical layers.
This image captures the western side-profile of Kinkaku-ji, right where the visitor pathway curves tightly around the structure along the edge of the pond. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
Originally constructed in 1397 as a retirement villa for Shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the pavilion complex was converted into a Zen temple following his death, in accordance with his final wishes. Yoshimitsu was the third shōgun of the Ashikaga shogunate, ruling from 1368 to 1394 during the Muromachi period. He is widely regarded as one of the era's most powerful and influential rulers, responsible for bringing the shogunate to the absolute peak of its political authority, diplomatic reach, and cultural sophistication.
From the 12th to the 19th centuries, the shōgun wielded supreme military and de facto political power in Japan. While the Emperor remained the official head of state and a sacred religious figure, the imperial court held no real governance; the shōgun ruled the country through a centralized military administration known as the shogunate.
Famous Zen Buddhist temple Kinkaku-ji located in Kyoto, Japan. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
Remarkably, Kinkaku-ji survived numerous fires and civil conflicts throughout the centuries, only to be tragically burned down in 1950 by a 22-year-old disgruntled Zen acolyte named Shōken Hayashi. This dramatic event later served as the centerpiece for Yukio Mishima’s acclaimed novel, The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. The structure standing today was meticulously reconstructed in 1955 to its original specifications, with its gold leaf layer further enhanced and thickened in the late 1980s.
This striking view captures Kinkaku-ji beautifully framed by vibrant purple Japanese water irises blooming along the edges of Mirror Pond (Kyoko-chi). Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
Upon studying the official literature, I later learned that the pavilion is a masterpiece of Muromachi architecture, uniquely blending three entirely distinct styles on each of its tiers. The first floor is built in the Shinden-zukuri style of 11th-century imperial palace architecture, characterized by natural unpainted wood walls and white plaster. The second floor follows the Bukke-zukuri style of samurai residences, completely sheathed in gold leaf and housing a sacred statue of Kannon Bodhisattva, the Buddhist deity of boundless compassion and mercy. The third floor is designed in the traditional Chinese Zen style (Zenshū-butsuden), heavily gilded inside and out, and topped with a radiant golden phoenix statue.
The main gate (Somon), which serves as the formal entrance to the Kinkaku-ji temple complex. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
On that September day, I visited some other nearby religious relics, but my time at Kinkaku-ji remained uniquely memorable. It was not just the brilliant hue of the pavilion that captivated me, but the surrounding grounds, which feature an authentic, masterfully designed strolling garden (kaiyūshiki-teien). The path winds gracefully past the Mirror Pond, showcasing small islets, meticulously placed rock formations gifted by regional lords, and natural springs. The central Kyōko-chi pond spans approximately 6,600 square meters and contains islands of various sizes, such as Ashihara-jima, alongside celebrated stone arrangements like the famous Hatakeyama rock.
The image shows the Sekkatei Teahouse, a historic Zen-style tea house located near the exit of the Kinkaku-ji temple garden. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
The compound is vast, and beyond the Golden Pavilion and Mirror Pond, there are numerous other details to admire: the rustic Sekkatei tea house, the reception hall grounds of the Hōjō (Abbot's Quarters), the serene Anmin-taku pond, several hidden springs and waterfalls, and grand entranceways like the Sōmon (Main Gate) and the Chinese-style Karamon gate.
This photo captures a close-up perspective from the edge of the Mirror Pond (Kyoko-chi), specifically facing a small fishing deck or veranda extension (Hosui-in) on the first floor of Kinkaku-ji. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
While many journey to Kinkaku-ji hoping to watch the sunset over its golden crest, timing makes a true twilight view difficult; the temple gates swing shut at 5pm, just before the sun dips below the horizon. Instead, the true reward is the legendary "golden hour illumination." In the late afternoon, the sun strikes the pavilion’s gold leaf at a perfect angle, casting a brilliant, fiery glow that mirrors flawlessly onto the water below. Pressed for time, I had to rush to my next destination, leaving the breathtaking spectacle to imagination—a radiant scene saved for another journey, and another lifetime.

item.title: Barman, Koch families allegedly left out of govt ethnic minority survey despite gazette recognition
item.description:
Many Barman and Koch families have allegedly been left out of a Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) survey on the socio-economic conditions and poverty of ethnic minority communities, despite being recognised in the government’s list of ethnic minority communities. The complaints raise questions about how that recognition is being applied during field-level data collection.
Community members from Thakurgaon and Panchagarh say they have faced inconsistent identity-verification requirements, with some families asked to produce certificates from the district administration to establish their ethnic identity.
In some cases, even when one family member holds a certificate and is included in the survey, their parents and siblings have been excluded. Others allege that Barmans holding certificates were recorded as “Bengali Barman Sanatan”.
Complaints have also emerged that Koch families in parts of Thakurgaon were excluded despite presenting certificates issued by the Tribal Welfare Association. Community members say they are unaware of any instruction requiring Koch people to produce such documents.
Anup Chandra Barman, a student at Hajee Mohammad Danesh Science and Technology University from Atwari upazila of Panchagarh, told Dhaka Tribune that only he was included in the survey from his four-member family, while his parents and sister were left out.
“The enumerator said only those with a certificate could be included in the survey. I asked him: if I am an ethnic minority member, does that mean my father, mother and sister are not? They also identify themselves as members of the community. Does having a certificate alone determine our identity?” he said.
Enumerator Bisu Kisku said he had followed instructions from higher authorities and entered the Barmans he surveyed as “Bengali Barman Sanatan” in the comments section.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
According to Anup, Kisku had included around 100 people from more than 90 families, but the community remained uncertain about how many of the households had ultimately been recorded.
A similar experience was reported by Pritilata Rani, a student at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University, whose family lives in Ruhia upazila of Thakurgaon. She told Dhaka Tribune that she contacted survey enumerator Sujan Pahan and was included, but her father, mother and sister were excluded because they did not have certificates from the district administration.
She said one member of the family was recognised as an ethnic minority for the survey while the other three were not, despite sharing the same family and community identity. She urged the authorities to consider their family and ethnic identity and ensure that all members were included.
The government recognised 50 ethnic minority communities through a gazette notification in 2019. The revised gazette, published on March 19 that year under the Small Ethnic Groups Cultural Institutions Act, 2010, lists Barman at serial number 15. The survey manual also lists the Barman and Koch communities separately.
The 2022 Population and Housing Census recorded 44,657 people as Barman and 13,702 as Koch in Bangladesh.
However, disagreements persist over the identity of some Barmans. While some identify themselves as Bengali or Kshatriya Barman, others assert a distinct ethnic minority identity. Community representatives say these differences have complicated their inclusion in the survey.
Sukanta Barman, a member of the Barman community in Thakurgaon, alleged that enumerators had been reluctant to collect information from Barman families. “Now we are in a deep hassle,” he said. “If anyone doesn’t want to be included, it’s fine, but if someone wants to be included in the survey, why can’t they?”
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
He said many community members had volunteered information on more than 90 families to enumerators, but the community did not know what had ultimately been entered into the survey tablets. Sukanta added that Koch families in the district had also been left out despite showing certificates issued by the Tribal Welfare Association.
“We want to be included in the survey, but someone or another does not want that. One obstacle after another is being created,” he said.
Researchers, however, said the issue needed to be understood in its historical context. Younger members of some families were reconnecting with their ancestral identity, they said, and urged that internal disagreements among organisations should not undermine government recognition.
Joba Rani Barman of Panchagarh said she had a certificate from the deputy commissioner but was recorded in the survey as “Bengali Barman Sanatan”.
Md Enamul Haque, deputy director of the Panchagarh District Statistics Office, said certificates from deputy commissioners had been sought to distinguish ethnic minority Barmans from Bengali Barmans. Some people had consequently been recorded as “Bengali Barman Sanatan”, he said.
Md Shafiqul Islam, joint director of the Rangpur Divisional Statistics Office, said officials assessed identity based on language, culture, traditions and other characteristics where certificates were unavailable. “Those identifying themselves as Bengali or Kshatriya Barman were not included as members of the ethnic minority community,” he said.
However, Md Faisal Hasan, acting deputy director of the Thakurgaon District Statistics Office, said Barmans holding certificates from the deputy commissioner had been included as ethnic minority members in his district.
The differing accounts have raised questions over whether the same identity-verification process was followed across districts.
Community members have also questioned the absence of Barman enumerators in the northern region, despite the survey plan’s stated intention to involve young students from ethnic minority communities in data collection. Thakurgaon district officials have said enumerator lists were prepared in consultation with local organisations and the administration.
Dinbandhu Barman, president of the Bangladesh Koch-Rajbanshi-Barman Organisation, said many Barman and Koch families had remained outside the survey. He said he had sought an extension of one week or more after the deadline was extended to October 30.
Farhana Sultana, project director of the survey and deputy director of the BBS’s PLS Cell, told Dhaka Tribune that although the programme was scheduled to end on October 30, information was still being collected from people who contacted the authorities.
“There have been some problems with verification. In such cases, we have to verify the information. We are also including those who have certificates from the district administration,” she said.
She said the certificate requirement had received particular attention in the case of Barmans because of disputes over identity within the community, unlike some other ethnic communities.
“Complaints are being reviewed,” Sultana said. People excluded due to errors involving surnames or national identity cards could apply through the deputy commissioner’s office, she said. “If their ancestors were identified as members of an ethnic minority community, their inclusion could be recommended.”
BBS Secretary Md Firoz Sarkar said complaints from Thakurgaon and Panchagarh would be examined after hearing the parties concerned.
The survey, titled “Survey on the Socio-economic Conditions and Poverty Situation of Ethnic Minority Communities 2026”, began on October 1 and was initially scheduled to continue until October 25. The deadline was later extended to October 30.

item.title: Bus set on fire in Baridhara
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to a passenger bus of Baishakhi Paribahan on Pragati Sarani in the Baridhara area of Dhaka on Friday evening. No casualties were reported, police said.
The incident occurred at around 5:45pm in Baridhara's J Block area.
According to sources at Bhatara police station, the bus operates on the Savar–Notun Bazar route. Shortly after dropping off passengers in the area, 2–3 miscreants allegedly set the bus on fire and fled the scene.
After being alerted, 2 units of the Fire Service from Baridhara Fire Station arrived and extinguished the blaze. Passengers managed to get off the bus safely before the fire spread, leaving no one injured.
Police sources said no clear closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage was available near the scene. Efforts are underway to identify those involved by examining footage from surrounding areas.
Bhatara police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Mazharul Islam said a police team visited the scene after the Fire Service brought the fire under control and moved the bus.
The bus driver and his assistant were taken to the police station for questioning in connection with the incident.
He added that police were working to identify and bring those responsible for setting the bus on fire to justice.

item.title: Tagore mural defaced with black ink in Khulna
item.description:
A mural of Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore at Khulna Railway Station has been defaced with black ink, drawing attention on Friday afternoon.
Officer-in-Charge of Khulna Sadar Police Station Lokman Hossain said police learned about the incident in the afternoon and launched an investigation.
“All businesses across the road were closed on Friday, making it difficult to determine who defaced the mural and when,” he said.
The murals were painted on the initiative of Khulna City Corporation (KCC) ahead of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to the city. They depict the July uprising, the Sundarbans, the Sixty Dome Mosque and the jute industry, alongside portraits of prominent figures who contributed to the region's art, literature and culture, including Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam.
A visit to the site revealed portraits of Fakir Lalon Shah, artist SM Sultan, Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, former prime minister Khaleda Zia, former president Ziaur Rahman and poet Michael Madhusudan Dutt on a wall beside Old Jessore Road. Tagore's was the only portrait defaced with black ink.
Two posters were also put up beside the mural.
One, titled “Opposition to the Establishment of Dhaka University”, featured several statements, including: “There is no place for Tagore, who was hostile to Muslims and East Bengal, in Titumir's Bengal. There is no place for glorifying India.”
Expressing outrage over the incident, KCC Administrator Nazrul Islam Manju said the portraits would help foster free thinking among children and adolescents.
“By defacing the portrait, they have exposed their narrow-mindedness and sick mentality,” he said.
Earlier, on October 10, the face of a Rabindranath Tagore mural in Dhaka was also defaced with black ink. Police detained four people in connection with the incident, including Al Nur Mohammad Ayash, member secretary of the State Dialogue Forum.

item.title: 15,550 yaba pills seized at Chittagong Central Jail in 10 months
item.description:
Inmates at Chittagong Central Jail are using unusual methods to smuggle yaba pills into the prison, including swallowing capsules wrapped in black tape and retrieving them after entering the facility.
The practice poses a serious health risk, as a capsule bursting inside an inmate's stomach could prove fatal. To prevent drug smuggling, jail authorities have intensified searches at three levels and begun keeping suspected smugglers separate from other inmates for at least two days.
According to jail sources, more than 500 drug consignments were seized at the prison between January and October this year, resulting in the recovery of 15,550 yaba pills.
Of the incidents, 44 involved large consignments and led to cases being filed with Kotwali police station. The pills were recovered from 44 inmates, including three women and 41 men. Disciplinary action was taken in other cases under prison regulations.
Jail authorities said the 15,550 yaba pills were recovered from 311 capsules over the 10-month period.
Drug use inside the prison is also a concern, with several inmates caught consuming narcotics. Officials suspect an organised network is facilitating drug smuggling and consumption within the facility.
Chittagong Central Jail Jailer Syed Shah Sharif said inmates swallow yaba capsules before entering the prison, while some attempt to conceal drugs in their rectums and other parts of their bodies. "Two to three drug consignments of varying sizes are intercepted almost every day. Numerous consignments have been seized over the past 10 months," he said.
He said searches had been intensified across prison wards and cells, with inmates undergoing multiple rounds of body searches before entry. "Officers check inmates from their mouths to different parts of their bodies. No one is allowed inside after just one search. They are screened at several points, both inside and outside the prison," he added.
Chittagong Central Jail Senior Jail Superintendent Md Iqbal Hossain said detecting drugs concealed inside the stomach through manual searches remained difficult. "Nevertheless, searches are conducted at three levels, starting at the prison entrance. Even a single Yaba capsule bursting inside an inmate's stomach could prove fatal," he said.
He added that cases were filed with the police station over major consignments, while disciplinary measures were taken in cases involving smaller quantities.
Kotwali police station Officer-in-Charge Zahedul Kabir said cases involving drug seizures inside the prison were being investigated seriously and necessary legal action was being taken.
Meanwhile, overcrowding has made drug control increasingly difficult at the prison. Against an official capacity of 2,249 inmates, the facility currently houses around 7,700, more than three times its capacity. At least 3,500 inmates are accused in cases under the Narcotics Control Act.
Prisons Department Chittagong Division Deputy Inspector General Md Sagir Mia said a dedicated narcotics prison was needed in the region. Keeping drug-addicted inmates and those accused in narcotics cases separate from ordinary prisoners would facilitate rehabilitation and help prevent the spread of drug use among other inmates, he said.

item.title: Home minister: People won’t allow AL to engage in politics again
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Friday ruled out the possibility of Awami League's return to politics, saying that the people would never again allow the party, which he described as oppressive, autocratic, fascist, and murderous, to engage in politics in the country.
"Those who shed people's blood to establish fascism, oppressed the people, and committed genocide will have no place in the country's politics again," he said while speaking at the concluding session of the 104th two-day annual religious conference at Babunagar Madrasa in Fatikchhari of Chittagong.
Questioning whether the people wanted the return of those he described as fascist forces, the minister said some were trying to create conditions for their comeback.
"Those who were forced to flee the country in the face of the mass uprising will not be allowed to return and engage in politics here," he said, adding that those responsible for mass killings and repression had yet to express regret or remorse.
Salahuddin said people were united in opposing the political activities of those responsible for mass killings, despite their differences in political views and ideologies. He also alleged that fascist forces were behind attempts to create unrest in the garment sector.
Addressing those who were creating trouble in the name of movements, the minister urged them to engage in constructive criticism. "You may choose not to cooperate with the government, but do not withhold your cooperation from the people of this country," he said.
He said it had taken 16 to 17 years to free the country from what he described as an autocratic and Islam-hostile regime. Salahuddin said many Islamic scholars and students had sacrificed their lives during the struggle.
Citing United Nations estimates, he said around 1,400 people had been killed during the July-August mass uprising, adding that nearly 3,000 people had been victims of enforced disappearance during the preceding 16 to 17 years.
"I was also one of them. By the grace of Almighty Allah and through people's prayers, I am still alive," the minister said.
He claimed that around 7,000 people had been killed or subjected to various forms of torture and persecution during that period, while millions had faced harassment through attacks and cases.
Salahuddin said they wanted the country to prosper economically and improve the living standards of Islamic scholars (ulema) and students of Qawmi madrasahs.
He also alleged that some groups use the name of Islam for political gain, although their election manifestos contain no mention of Islamic values. “Although they say one thing, their documents and official records tell a different story,” he said.
"We believe in Islamic values. We are the party that included 'Bismillah' in the Constitution. We follow the nationalist and Islamic values introduced by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman," the minister said.
"We have built a united Bangladesh where people from all walks of life share a common national identity. We never want to see division among the people of this country," he added.

item.title: Zahid: Govt working to ensure free primary healthcare for all
item.description:
Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Minister Prof Dr AZM Zahid Hossain on Friday said the government is working to ensure free primary healthcare services for all citizens.
"The government is taking pragmatic steps to ensure that general patients can receive quality and modern medical treatment at divisional and regional levels without having to travel to the capital," he said.
The minister made the remarks while addressing the 32nd National Conference and 2nd Outreach Program of Bangladesh Society of Radiology and Imaging as the chief guest at Shaheed Abu Sayed International Convention Centre in the capital.
Dr Zahid said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had allocated the highest-ever budget for the health sector in the current fiscal year. "We must ensure proper utilisation of this budget for the overall development of the country's healthcare system," he said, adding that despite resource constraints, a significant transformation in healthcare could be achieved through sincerity, efficiency and effective use of available resources.
Assuring the government's support through necessary funding and policy directives to improve healthcare quality, the minister said bringing qualitative changes to the medical sector was a collective responsibility of all stakeholders.
He urged medical professionals to work together to ensure that patients could receive comprehensive treatment for complex diseases within the country, without having to seek medical care abroad. He also called for proper career planning to prepare young doctors for future leadership roles in the medical sector.
Meanwhile, speakers at the conference said liver cirrhosis ranked seventh among the top 10 causes of death in Bangladesh. Around seven million people in the country are infected with Hepatitis B, while more than 45 million adults suffer from fatty liver disease, they said.
They warned that 40 to 60% of patients die within a year when the condition becomes critical, stressing the importance of early diagnosis and public awareness.
The speakers also called for avoiding unnecessary CT scans and surgeries and urged the introduction of radiation risk allowance for healthcare professionals in Bangladesh, similar to that in other countries.
The conference was chaired by Brigadier General (retd) Dr Sayed Awsaf Ali, while Bangladesh Society of Radiology and Imaging General Secretary Professor Dr Md Nazrul Islam delivered the welcome address.
Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr F M Siddiqui attended the event as the special guest.
Delegates, expert physicians and researchers from several countries, including India, Pakistan, the Netherlands, South Korea and the United States, took part in the conference.

Food, medicine shortages choke 3,000 patients at Barisal hospital
item.description:
Around 3,000 inpatients at Barisal Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital face the risk of losing their daily meals as the institution has received no government allocation for food supplies since July.
The hospital, which has 1,000 beds, treats around 5,000 patients daily, including 2,500–3,000 inpatients and more than 2,000 outpatient visitors.
Hospital authorities have so far managed to continue food supplies through the contractor at the director’s request. However, eggs were dropped from patients’ meals on October 15 to reduce costs. The director warned that food supplies could be suspended from March if the government allocation does not arrive.
Hospital Director Brigadier General Dr AKM Mashiul Munir told Bangla Tribune that the contractor had been asked to continue supplying meals despite the lack of funds since July.
“We have reduced the food cost by Tk15 per patient. There was no scope to remove anything else from the menu except eggs. Eggs will be added again once the allocation arrives. If the government funding does not come, we will have no option but to stop food supplies from March,” he said.
The hospital is the main healthcare facility for people across the six districts of Barisal Division, while patients from neighbouring districts also seek treatment there.
Despite its 1,000-bed capacity, around 3,000 patients are admitted daily. More than 1,000 patients receive treatment on floors, while additional beds have been arranged in corridors, balconies and open spaces. Even critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) sometimes have to receive treatment on the floor.
The director said 978 additional beds had been arranged in open spaces to improve patient management.
With two to three attendants accompanying each patient, around 10,000 people are present at the hospital daily, disrupting movement and the treatment environment.
Patients are also facing shortages of essential medicines and diagnostic supplies. X-ray films and medicines required for thyroid tests are unavailable, while CT scans have remained suspended due to a lack of necessary supplies despite the machine being operational.
Medicines for cancer and other complex diseases have also been in short supply for a long time, while some major surgeries cannot be performed.
Hospital sources said the monthly government allocation is insufficient to cover even 11 days of expenses for the current patient load.
Eight of the hospital’s 13 lifts are also out of order. Five of the nine lifts in the old building and three of the four in the new building are non-functional, making it difficult to move patients between floors.
Relatives often have to wait for long periods to take critically ill patients on trolleys to different floors.
Munir blamed the Public Works Department (PWD) for delays in repairing the lifts, saying repeated requests had failed to resolve the problem.
However, PWD Sub-divisional Engineer Md Rasheduzzaman said estimates for the repairs had already been sent to the relevant authorities. Work would begin after funding approval and the appointment of a contractor through a tender process.
The director also expressed concern over declining hospital revenue, blaming irregularities among staff and the outsourcing of diagnostic tests that could be conducted in-house.
He said the hospital should conduct tests on around 1,100 patients daily but currently manages only 500, despite having a target of 2,000.
As a result, hospital revenue has fallen by half compared with the previous year, he added.
Munir said he had taken several initiatives to restore discipline, including arranging additional beds and reorganising wards, but a lack of cooperation had hindered progress.

item.title: Garment workers' protests: 47 cases of disinformation, including claims of killings and shootings, identified
item.description:
A video showing two children crying after losing their mother has been circulating on Facebook. The caption claims that “BNP terrorists, along with police, attacked and killed a female garment worker and made her body disappear. Her family members, including a small child, are seen crying helplessly.”

However, a fact-check found that the video does not show relatives mourning a female worker killed during the ongoing labour protests. It shows an incident involving Sumi Akter (27) a garment worker who suddenly fell ill while working at the Agami Fashion Ltd factory of Deco Group in Savar’s Noapara, Ashulia, on 16 October. She was taken to the Women and Children Hospital in Ashulia, where the attending physician declared her dead.

Garment workers have been staging protests in several industrial areas, including Mirpur, Savar-Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000. Clashes and chases between workers and police have also taken place in several areas during the demonstrations. Amid this situation, various forms of misinformation have been spreading on social media.

Some posts claim that several workers were killed by police gunfire, while others describe injured people as having been shot. AI-generated images and videos, edited news cards, fake statements and old photos and videos from unrelated incidents are also being circulated as part of the ongoing protests.

Fact-checking organisations have been publishing reports on misinformation surrounding the garment workers’ demonstrations. As of 12pm on Friday, three fact-checking organisations had identified and reported 47 such incidents. Rumor Scanner reported 33, Dismislab eight and BanglaFact six.

False claims of workers being killed

Several claims that workers had been killed have circulated on social media amid the garment workers’ protests. From 4 November, Facebook posts claimed that five workers had been shot dead in Hemayetpur. A day earlier, posts claimed that eight workers had been killed and more than 100 injured in Ashulia in police firing. Other posts alleged that two or four workers had been killed in Gazipur and Mirpur.

Verification shows no evidence to support the claims that five workers had been shot dead in Hemayetpur or eight in Ashulia. The claims of workers being killed in Gazipur and Mirpur were also false.

An analysis of the viral posts found no reliable information or evidence to support these claims. There were no reports from the police or news media confirming that several workers had been killed by police gunfire in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia or Mirpur. Police press releases and media reports also contained no information supporting the claims.

However, not all reports of casualties during the protests were false. Garment worker Toufiq Hossain, who was injured in Gazipur, died while undergoing treatment on 3 November. No information was found about anyone being killed in the clashes in Hemayetpur.

Injured people falsely described as having been shot

There have also been instances of injured people being falsely described as victims of gunfire during the protests. A photograph circulated with the claim that a worker named Tanjina Akter Shormi had been shot the previous day and died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital.

However, verification found that the woman in the photograph was not Tanjina Akter Shormi but Jannat. She had not been shot either. She had fallen ill after being exposed to tear gas shells fired by police in Fatullah. Video footage obtained during the fact-check showed her getting back on her feet later.

Another claim, circulated on Facebook and several other platforms, said that a class-V student of BKSP School was in critical condition after being shot by police while returning home during the garment workers’ protests.

The claim was shared not only by accounts supportive of the Awami League but also by Facebook groups supportive of Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party. However, speaking to the student’s father, Yusuf Rana, fact-checkers learned that a piece of brick had struck his son on the head from behind as he was leaving school after classes. The student was injured, but there was no incident of him being shot.

Misleading claim that factories have been shut down

A video has circulated with the claim that all factories of Pacific Jeans Ltd, a jeans manufacturer, have been shut down. The video shows workers inside a factory hugging one another and crying.

However, verification found that the claim was false. Production has been stopped at an old building of Unit 1 of Pacific Jeans Ltd. The company has taken a policy decision to demolish the building. Production continues at its other units and at the other factories of Pacific Jeans Group.

AI-generated images and videos spread to mislead

AI-generated images and videos have also been circulated amid the workers’ protests. A video was shared with the claim that a garment factory in Mirpur had been attacked and vandalised. Another was circulated with the claim that “police are firing on garment workers' processions under Tarique Rahman's orders”.

A third video shows a police officer holding a gun and firing towards a crowd. It was also claimed to show police shooting at workers.

However, verification found that none of the three videos was authentic. All had been created using AI.

A photograph was also circulated with the claim that BNP leaders and activists had taken to the streets with firearms alongside police to suppress the protests. It shows several people standing with weapons in their hands, with police officers behind them.

Verification found that the photograph was not real. An image of BNP leaders and activists standing with sticks in Mirpur had been edited using AI. Firearms were added to their hands and images of police officers were placed in the background.

False claims spread through edited news cards

Edited news cards bearing the logos of media outlets have also been circulated amid the garment workers’ protests. A news card carrying the logo of a television channel was shared with the claim that Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed had said, “If the workers do not stop protesting, they will meet the same fate as the Awami League.”

Another news card was circulated on Facebook with the claim that garment workers had announced a “Long March to Dhaka” programme.

Verification found no evidence that the home minister had made the quoted remark. The card had been created by digitally editing a different news card from the television channel.

Similarly, there was no information that protesting workers had announced a “Long March to Dhaka”. A different news card had been digitally edited and circulated to support the claim.

A Facebook page also posted a claim on 5 November that 20 people had been killed, more than 2,000 injured and over 500 arrested in five days of garment workers’ protests. Verification found that the claims of 20 deaths and more than 2,000 injuries were false. The figure of more than 500 arrests was also exaggerated.

Fake quotes attributed to prominent figures

Fake quotes attributed to prominent political and government figures have also been circulated in connection with the protests. A news card carrying a photograph of Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, political adviser to the prime minister on industries and acting secretary general of the BNP, was shared with the claim that he had said, “Each one of them are garment workers but are demanding an officer’s salary.”

Another news card attributed a statement to Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, claiming he had said, “There are no genuine workers in this movement, they are mainly trying to destabilise the country for political purposes.” The card also claimed that he had urged party leaders and activists to take action against the protesters.

Verification found that neither quote was true. No reliable evidence was found that either of the two people holding important government positions had made such remarks. In fact, the quotes originated from posts created by a satirical Facebook page called “Gupto TV” and were circulated as genuine comments.

Videos from unrelated incidents circulated as protest footage

Videos of various incidents unrelated to the ongoing labour protests have been circulated with new claims. A video was shared with the claim that a female garment worker had been tied to a tree to prevent her from joining the protests. Some posts claimed that a JCD leader in Kaliakair upazila had tied her up.

However, verification found that the video was nearly three months old. It shows the daughter-in-law of an elderly woman being tied up in Mymensingh in August 2026 over allegations that she had murdered the elderly woman.

Another video was circulated under the headline, “Police enter a mosque wearing shoes while prayers are underway to search for garment workers.” Verification found that the footage had no connection with the ongoing garment workers’ protests. It shows police entering a mosque during an eviction drive against hawkers in Mirpur-10 in Dhaka on 30 September.

Old BNP footage circulated

A photograph was circulated on Facebook amid the workers’ protests with the claim that a BNP leader had attacked the demonstrations in Gazipur with a heavy firearm.

Verification found that the photograph was not related to any attack on garment workers. It shows a man carrying a firearm and chasing members of the opposing group during a clash between two factions of the BNP in Sitakunda, Chattogram, on 2 September this year, ahead of the party’s founding anniversary.

A video was also circulated under the headline, “The prime minister himself takes to the streets during the garment workers’ movement.”

However, verification found that the video had no connection with the recent garment workers’ protests. On 22 October, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman visited Mongla and stepped out of his vehicle, breaking protocol, to mingle with ordinary people. The video is from that visit.

Videos from the July uprising circulated

A video was circulated with the claim that it showed an injured worker speaking during the ongoing garment workers’ protests. In the footage, a man appears to fall ill after being exposed to a tear gas shell. He is heard saying, “Even if I die, you must not back down.”

However, the video is neither from the garment workers’ protests nor recent. It is an old video of a man who fell ill after being hit by a tear gas shell during the July uprising in 2024, now being circulated with a new claim.

Videos of unrelated political programmes linked to workers’ protests

A video was circulated with the claim that people were being paid to join the garment workers’ protests. Verification found that it had no connection with the demonstrations. It shows a scene from the Inqilab Moncho’s “March for Justice” programme.

A photograph was also circulated with the claim that it showed a worker killed by police gunfire in Savar on 4 November. However, verification found that the image was of a young man named Ahad Ahmed, who was killed in an attack by his cousins over a land dispute in Rampal, Bagerhat, on 21 September.

Another photograph was shared with the claim that BNP-Jamaat terrorists had hacked a garment worker to death on suspicion that he was a Jubo League supporter. Verification found that the image was not from the recent workers’ protests. It shows the killing of Jubo League leader Zubayer Parvez in Feni last June.

Old Photographs circulated

On 4 November, a photograph of a dead man was circulated on Facebook with the claim that “a worker was killed by police gunfire in Savar just a while ago”. Former State Minister for Information and Broadcasting Mohammad Ali Arafat also shared the claim on his Facebook profile.

However, verification found that the photograph did not show a worker killed by police in Savar on 4 November. It was a photograph of a young man named Ahad Ahmed, who was killed in an attack by his cousins over a land dispute in Rampal, Bagerhat, on 21 September.

Another photograph was circulated with the claim that BNP-Jamaat terrorists had hacked a garment worker to death on suspicion that he was a Jubo League supporter. However, verification found that the photograph was unrelated to the recent workers’ protests. It showed the killing of Jubo League leader Zubayer Parvez in Feni last June.

Fake list of the new wage structure

Following garment workers’ protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000, the Minimum Wage Board was formed on 1 November. Subsequently, a new wage list was circulated on Facebook under the title “Gazette for garment workers”, bearing the name of the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The posts claimed that it was the new wage structure for garment workers.

However, verification found that the list was not the new wage structure. Although the board has been formed to set a new minimum wage, discussions have taken place about determining the new wages for garment workers in December.

A meeting of the Minimum Wage Board was held at its office in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, on 4 November. The meeting was chaired by the board’s new chairman, Syed Azad Subhani. After the meeting, he told journalists that the workers’ and employers’ representatives would submit separate wage proposals at the board’s second meeting. The independent member would also submit a proposal. The board would then discuss the proposals.

No news reports or other information about the publication of a new wage structure for garment workers were found in the media. No related post was found on the Facebook page of the Ministry of Labour and Employment either.

False claim about Ha-Meem Group chairman's arrest

A claim circulated on Facebook linking the garment workers’ protests to the arrest of Ha-Meem Group chairman and former MP AK Azad. One post said his arrest had caused a stir in the country’s industrial and business sectors. It also raised questions about the reasons for his arrest, details of the case and the next legal steps.

However, verification found that the claim of Ha-Meem Group chairman AK Azad’s arrest was false. The claim was circulated without any reliable information or evidence.

45th BCS: 45 candidates do not join education cadre despite being gazetted
item.description:
Although 45 candidates were finally gazetted for the education cadre through the 45th Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination, they did not join their jobs.

The joining process for the 45th BCS education cadre has ended, leaving 45 posts vacant.

The Secondary and Higher Education Division of the Ministry of Education issued a gazette in this regard last Thursday (5 November).

The gazette said that the joining letters of 339 lecturers who submitted their joining letters for the lecturer posts had been accepted, effective from their respective dates of joining. As many as 25 lecturers joined in Bangla, 23 in English, 19 in political science, 14 in philosophy, 17 in economics and 18 in zoology.

In addition, 12 joined in history, nine in social welfare, 23 in chemistry, five in psychology, 20 in Islamic history and culture, 17 in physics, 18 in botany, six in sociology, 17 in mathematics, eight in geography, two in soil science, 18 in accounting, five in marketing, 19 in management, two in finance and banking, five in agricultural science, three in statistics, one in resource management and entrepreneurship, one in institutional food management, and 32 as lecturers in information and communication technology.

Earlier, on 25 October 2026, the Ministry of Education issued a notification appointing 384 candidates to the BCS (General Education) cadre through the 45th BCS examination, subject to 14 conditions. The gazette required the appointed candidates to be physically present at the Rural Development Academy (RDA) in Bogura by 1 November to join their posts. Following the notification, 339 candidates joined, the Ministry of Education said.

item.title: PM pays tribute to Ziaur Rahman, Khaleda Zia on Nat'l Revolution and Solidarity Day
item.description:
Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman today, Saturday paid homage at the graves of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia at Zia Udyan in Dhaka, marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.

Accompanied by senior party leaders, the Prime Minister arrived at around 8:30 am, offered prayers and took part in a special munajat seeking eternal peace for the departed souls. He then laid wreaths at the graves and stood in silence for a while.

BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Social Welfare and Women and Children Affairs Minister Prof Dr A Z M Zahid Hossain, Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Aazam Khan, and Chief Whip Nurul Islam Moni, among others, were present.

Meanwhile, BNP has organised a procession in the capital to mark the day. The procession is scheduled to start at 3:00 pm in front of the party's central office in Nayapaltan, with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman expected to take part on foot.

Rizvi said the procession would pass the Chief Justice's residence in Kakrail, the Hotel InterContinental intersection, Banglamotor and Farmgate before ending at Manik Mia Avenue.

According to party sources, Tarique Rahman's expected participation has generated enthusiasm among party leaders and activists. BNP's Dhaka North and Dhaka South city units and affiliated organisations have made extensive preparations for the programme.

item.title: Time to reclaim Noakhali, Chittagong Port, Sylhet regions along with PoK: BJP MP Nishikant Dubey
item.description:
ANI_20261022301

Indian ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP Nishikant Dubey on Friday said that it was time for India to "reclaim" Noakhali, Chittagong Port and Sylhet region, along with Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), that were "forcibly handed over" by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru.

Dubey said that these three areas were part of the Tipra Kingdom.

"The time has come not just to reclaim Pakistan-occupied Kashmir from Pakistan. It is also time to reclaim the territories that Nehru ji forcibly handed over, whether it is Noakhali, Chittagong Port or Sylhet," Dubey told ANI.

The BJP leader claimed that the then Tripura King Bir Bikram Singh questioned then PM Nehru over "negotiations over his territory".

"The three areas, Noakhali, Sylhet and Chittagong Port, were part of the Tipra Kingdom. Tripura was earlier known as Tipra. Its king, Bir Bikram Singh, was continuously fighting with Nehru, questioning how he could negotiate over his territory. He would ask: How can you hand over Noakhali to Pakistan? How can you hold a referendum on Sylhet? How can you hold a referendum on Chittagong? This is my kingdom. I will decide whether it remains part of India, Pakistan or becomes an independent state," Dubey said.

"Sardar Patel sent the Army, and Tripura became part of India in October 1948. Maharani Kanchan Prabha signed the Instrument of Accession in October 1948, following which Tripura became part of India," he added.

Dubey alleged that Pandit Nehru prioritised bringing the Muslim League into his government over responding to the violence against Hindus in Noakhali in 1946, claiming that around 10,000 Hindus were killed in the massacre.

"Nehru ji was desperate to become Prime Minister. India became independent in 1947, but he did not become Prime Minister on August 15, 1947. He became Prime Minister on September 2, 1946. As soon as he became Prime Minister, the Muslim League started Direct Action," the BJP MP said.

In October, on October 15, 1946, a massive massacre of Hindus took place in Noakhali, a Hindu-majority area. Around 10,000 Hindus were killed in a single day. But he did not go there as Prime Minister. He remained concerned about how the Muslim League could become part of his government," he added.

Dubey further said that the going away of Chittagong Port was responsible for the halt in development of the entire northeast.

"It was precisely because Chittagong Port went away that the development of the entire Northeast was halted. If the Northeast appears backwards today, if it faces problems, if we are unable to fully utilise its mines, minerals and gas, and if the region still feels disconnected, it is only because we no longer have that port. This is the time to reclaim Chittagong, Noakhali and Sylhet as well," he asserted.

Dubet said that the person, Baharul Islam, who conducted the Sylhet referendum was made a Rajya Sabha member by Congress.

"Nehru ji wanted to become Prime Minister by any means. When the King of Tripura, or the Maharani, decided in 1948 that they wanted to remain with India, and there was a year-long struggle in Tripura between 1947 and 1948, how could you hand over its territories, including the Hindu-majority areas of Chittagong, Noakhali and Sylhet, to Pakistan, which is now Bangladesh? Who gave you this right?" Dubey stated.

"The person who conducted the Sylhet referendum-do you know Baharul Islam? The Congress made him a Rajya Sabha member. After he left the Rajya Sabha, he was appointed a High Court judge. After retiring as a High Court judge, he was appointed a Supreme Court judge. After retiring from the Supreme Court, the Congress again made him a Rajya Sabha member," he said.

Dubey informed that Baharul Islam was a member of the Muslim League Red Army, which was involved in the Noakhali massacre and played a major role in securing Chittagong and conducting the Sylhet referendum.

"Now is the time to correct history. Just as Pakistan-occupied Kashmir is under Pakistan's control and the time has come to reclaim it, the time has also come to reclaim Chittagong Port, Sylhet and Noakhali in the Northeast," he said.

His remarks come as TIPRA Motha Party founder Pradyot Bikram Manikya Deb Barma alleged that "huge parts of erstwhile Tripura Kingdom was seceded to east Pakistan keeping my Grandmother in the dark during partition and this was the darkest period in our nations history".

"Today if we had sea access we would no longer be worried about the chickens neck . This strategic blunder by the then Government-of India has cost not just the state of Tripura/Northeast and the nation itself . Our Greater tipraland movement has often been maligned but the real intention has always been to assimilate those parts which were cut off by historical blunders of the past," Mankiya, titular king and head of the royal house of Tripura, posted on X.
