item.title: Tk 800 million spent developing 12 software tools: How useful have they been?
item.description:
On 15 December last year, Faiz Ahmad Taiyeb, special assistant to the chief adviser of the former interim government, launched an artificial intelligence (AI) platform called Kagoj.ai. One of the services offered by the platform is optical character recognition (OCR), which can convert text in images or documents into editable Word files.

Speaking as the chief guest at the launch ceremony, Taiyeb said, “We want to make the best use of technology to make language accessible. By leveraging various opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, people will be able to use the different features of Kagoj Tools.”

However, the government service appears to have very limited usage. Meanwhile, Google Lens, available on almost everyone's smartphone, can easily convert text from images or documents into editable Word files. Many other apps also offer this service free of charge. These apps were launched long before the government introduced Kagoj.ai.

The Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Division has spent Tk 800 million developing 12 software tools to facilitate the use of Bangla in information technology. These include tools for converting audio into text, correcting spelling and grammar, and translating Bangla into other languages, among others. The development process has taken 10 years.

The project, titled Enrichment of Bangla Language in Information Technology through Research and Development, was launched in 2016 under the Awami League government. It is being implemented by the Bangladesh Computer Council (BCC), an agency under the ICT Division. The project has an allocation of Tk 1.58 billion, funded by the government. Its tenure has been extended three times, most recently in August, when the deadline was extended to June 2028.

People familiar with the matter say the new government should have reviewed projects undertaken by the Awami League government in the ICT sector, scrapped most of them and ensured accountability of those involved. Instead, the project tenures are being extended.

Asked about the project, ICT Secretary Md Mamunur Rashid Bhuiyan told Prothom Alo, “Several tools have been developed under the Bangla language enrichment project. However, I would not say that all of them have been particularly meaningful. The tools have not reached people in the way they were supposed to.”

He added, “We are working on bringing the tools together on a single platform and making them user-friendly so that people can access them.”

The secretary also said that ongoing projects in the ICT sector had not been discontinued. Rather, the authorities had reviewed which projects needed to continue and to what extent they were justified.

“We have reassessed the scope of 10 to 12 projects and dropped the components that we considered unnecessary,” he said.

However, the expenditure on the Bangla language enrichment project in information technology has not been reduced under the current government.

How much has been spent, how many people are using the tools?

The project titled Enrichment of Bangla Language in Information Technology through Research and Development initially envisaged developing 16 software applications, tools and technological resources. According to people involved in the project, work on 12 components has been completed over the past 10 years. However, not all of these services are fully operational or easily accessible to the general public.

Various Bangla-language software and services developed under the project are available on the website bangla.gov.bd. An AI assistant named 'Jiggasha' has been introduced to provide information about government services. Other initiatives include a screen reader for visually impaired people, sign language recognition, a Braille converter, a database of languages spoken by ethnic minority communities, and Bangla fonts and keyboards.

According to project sources, around Tk 800 million has been spent so far. Of this, Tk 600 million has gone towards software development, hosting and maintenance. The remaining amount has been spent on office decoration, meetings, seminars, campaigns and operational costs.

Concerned persons say these software applications and technologies are still at a preliminary stage. An investigation is needed to determine how much expenditure was shown for developing each tool and how much was actually spent.

An analysis of usage data for the different services under the project shows considerable variations in their popularity. For example, the AI chatbot 'Jiggasha', designed to provide information about government services, receives an average of 110 requests a day during its trial run. Meanwhile, the font conversion service processed 275 files over 35 days. The Bangla spelling checker receives around 500,000 requests a day on average, while the OCR service on Kagoj.ai receives about 50 requests daily.

To assess the effectiveness of these technologies developed by the ICT Division, Prothom Alo tested several tools at different times over the past month.

The tests found that the Bangla spelling checker performed quite well. However, the audio-to-text service encountered problems when processing large files. The AI-powered chatbot Jiggasha could answer general questions but sometimes provided misleading information in response to complex queries.

Project officials said the existing GPU capacity allows the services to cater to only a limited number of users simultaneously. A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialised computer processor used to run artificial intelligence models and process large volumes of data quickly.

Officials claim that the existing capacity can serve between 5,000 and 10,000 users simultaneously across the different services. However, users may have to wait when demand is high. As a result, additional GPUs and infrastructure are needed to make the services widely accessible to the general public.

The question is: if technologies developed at a cost of nearly Tk 1.58 billion cannot be made suitable for public use because of inadequate infrastructure, who will keep them operational after the project ends?

Asked about this, project director Mahbub Karim told Prothom Alo that the technology and databases would be handed over to the Bangladesh Computer Council after the project was completed. He said there would also be scope to purchase additional GPUs or increase capacity as needed in the future.

Past experience, however, has not been encouraging. During the Awami League government's tenure, a Tk 3.3 billion project was undertaken to develop mobile games and applications. Most of the games and apps developed under that project proved useless. People familiar with the matter said the projects were undertaken largely to award contracts to people close to those in power. More than 17 per cent of the total project expenditure went towards making films and games named after members of the Sheikh family.

Those involved in the Bangla language enrichment project argue that its objectives are different. They say its significance lies not merely in developing software but also in creating the databases necessary for advancing artificial intelligence and language technology in Bangla.

According to them, around 8,000 copyright-free books have been digitised under the project. They have also developed 10,000 hours of audio data for converting spoken Bangla into text and 1,000 hours of audio data for converting text into speech. In addition, more than 12,000 minutes of audio recordings in 44 languages spoken by ethnic minority communities and 42,800 sign language videos have been collected.

Experts, however, say the project's success cannot be judged solely by the number of software applications developed or the volume of data collected. The key considerations should be how widely these technologies are being used, how effective they are and how long they will remain operational after the project ends.

A 'wasteful' project

During the Awami League government's tenure, which ended following the July mass uprising, 21 projects were undertaken in the ICT sector in the name of building Digital Bangladesh. According to the ICT Division, the approved expenditure for these projects totalled nearly Tk 190 billion.

A 12-member committee was formed on 28 August 2024 to evaluate the projects. In its report, the committee said some projects included activities that had little or no connection with their stated objectives. Others contained components that did not fall under the jurisdiction of the ICT Division. The committee estimated that Tk 6.981 billion could be saved by removing unnecessary components.

The projects were undertaken in the name of developing apps, providing freelancing training, building ICT infrastructure, setting up IT parks and establishing incubation centres. Former ICT State Minister Zunaid Ahmed Palak faced the most allegations of irregularities and corruption in connection with these projects. He is now in prison. Many others involved in the projects have yet to be held accountable.

Asked about the matter, Professor BM Mainul Hossain of the Institute of Information Technology at the University of Dhaka told Prothom Alo that there were widespread allegations of irregularities and corruption in various ICT sector projects.

“Simply extending project deadlines without examining past practices and project outcomes amounts to condoning the activities of the previous administration,” he said.

item.title: ‘Coordinator’ of attack, Juboraj, still not arrested
item.description:
More than a month has passed since the attack on the New Gini Properties Limited project at ECB Chattar in the capital. However, the Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Detective Branch (DB) has yet to arrest Md Juboraj, whom investigators have identified as one of the key coordinators of the attack.

According to sources involved in the investigation, Juboraj, a member of the gang led by Md Ibrahim, convenor of Bhashantek thana BNP, also known as “killer” Ibrahim, coordinated the attack by bringing together members of two criminal gangs in Mirpur.

He is allegedly involved in various criminal activities in the Mirpur area on Ibrahim's behalf.

A source involved in the investigation said that 13 people sat down at a food shop in the ECB Chattar area at noon on the day of the attack to plan the operation.

At that time, Shahriar Mahmud, the prime accused in the case, contacted Md Ibrahim and agreed to pay him Tk 10 million (1 crore) for carrying out the attack. Ibrahim subsequently recruited people and assigned Juboraj to lead the operation.

Investigators have identified nine more people allegedly involved in the attack and are trying to arrest them. So far, police have arrested 11 people on allegations of planning and directly participating in the attack. Eight of them have secured bail.

Inspector Jehad Hossain of the DB's Gulshan Division, the investigation officer in the case, told Prothom Alo that more than 100 people had taken part in the attack. Investigators have identified many of them and are trying to arrest them.

The attack on the New Gini Properties housing project took place on the night of 26 September. During the incident, attackers also vandalised and looted content creator Salman Muqtadir's studio.

On the night of the attack, Salman posted a video on social media describing what had happened. The incident subsequently sparked widespread reactions in various quarters.

Criminal gang hired for Tk 10 million

The attackers allegedly hired a criminal gang for Tk 10 million (1 crore) to carry out the assault on the New Guinea housing project.

According to sources familiar with the matter, Md Ibrahim, convenor of Bhashantek Thana BNP, arranged the attack by sending people in exchange for money. Members of Mamun's gang in Mirpur also took part in the operation.

Investigators said they obtained this information by questioning Shahriar Mahmud and Bikash Chandra Sarkar, who were arrested in connection with the attack.

According to the investigators, Shahriar and Bikash were present when the group planned the attack at a food shop in the ECB Chattar area. Shahriar Mahmud is currently out on bail.

A visit to the site on 3 November found construction work underway at several buildings inside the New Gini housing project, with workers continuing their duties.

However, Salman Muqtadir's studio, which sustained damage during the attack, has yet to undergo repairs. Equipment and other belongings remain scattered across the floor.

At a special screening of a film at Star Cineplex in SKS Tower, Mohakhali, Dhaka, on 31 October, Salman Muqtadir said that he would no longer invest in Bangladesh.

“Promise” of a free flat

The investigation into the attack has brought to light a dispute over 35 kathas of land adjacent to the housing project. The dispute centres on the use of a road through the New Gini project to access the land.

Investigators said Major General (retd) Golam Mohiuddin Chowdhury also owns land within the 35-katha plot. He was trying to develop a condominium there.

However, the land has no access road. Constructing residential buildings there would serve little purpose unless the owner of the New Gini project provided a road for access.

Investigators believe the attackers planned the assault to demolish the main gate of the New Gini housing project and create an access road.

According to sources involved in the investigation, Shahriar was assigned to break down the gate during the attack and create an access road.

In return, Mohiuddin Chowdhury allegedly promised him a flat in the building planned for the plot as a gift. He also promised to award him the contract to supply bricks and sand for the construction work.

Police arrested Mohiuddin Chowdhury in connection with the case and took him into remand for questioning. He was later granted bail.

Project owner alleges death threats

Following the attack, allegations have emerged that Md Nazim Uddin Bhuiyan, owner of the New Gini housing project, has received death threats. He claims that people have threatened him in various ways.

Nazim Uddin Bhuiyan told Prothom Alo that he had filed a general diary (GD) with the police seeking security for his life. He said, “The accused are threatening me after securing bail. Criminals are also threatening to shoot and kill me through various intermediaries. I fear for my life.”

Claiming that he has no affiliation with any political party, he said he was a businessman. He alleged that during the Awami League government's tenure, authorities filed cases against him, accusing him of being involved in BNP-Jamaat politics. Now, he said, they were filing cases against him by labelling him a fascist.

item.title: Ziaur Rahman’s photo missing from banner, Sheikh Mujib called ‘Father of the Nation’, sparking uproar
item.description:
An uproar broke out at a discussion in Joypurhat marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day after the banner was found to be missing a photograph of martyred President Ziaur Rahman, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was referred to as ‘Bangabandhu’ and the ‘Father of the Nation’.

State Minister for Public Administration and Food Abdul Bari expressed anger over the incident and ordered an investigation into it. Deputy Commissioner of Joypurhat Al-Mamun Mia has apologised in this regard.

The meeting, organised by the district administration, was scheduled to begin at 10:00 am today, Saturday, at the District Shilpakala Academy. However, the programme could not start at the scheduled time because the banner did not feature a photograph of Ziaur Rahman.

After Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders and activists expressed their anger, a poster bearing his photograph was attached to the banner with adhesive tape, and then the meeting began.

During the meeting, Maruf Hasan, general secretary of the Joypurhat municipality unit of the Zia Parishad, spoke about the significance of National Revolution and Solidarity Day. In his speech, he repeatedly referred to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman as the ‘Father of the Nation’ and ‘Bangabandhu’. This triggered uproar at the venue.

Speaking to eyewitnesses and BNP leaders and activists, it was learnt that State Minister Abdul Bari arrived at the venue before the scheduled time. BNP leaders and activists informed him that the banner did not feature a photograph of Ziaur Rahman. The state minister therefore did not go up on to the stage.

Later, Deputy Commissioner Al-Mamun Mia and other officials went on to the stage and attached a poster bearing Ziaur Rahman’s photograph to the banner with adhesive tape. The state minister then took his place on the stage, and the discussion meeting began half an hour behind schedule.

During the meeting, Maruf Hasan, general secretary of the Joypurhat municipality unit of the Zia Parishad, spoke about the significance of National Revolution and Solidarity Day. In his speech, he repeatedly referred to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman as the ‘Father of the Nation’ and ‘Bangabandhu’. This triggered uproar at the venue.

At one point, district Chhatra Dal unit president AKM Golam Mahfuz became agitated and rushed towards the dais on the stage. Maruf Hasan was eventually removed from the dais, and the meeting resumed after that. State Minister Abdul Bari was present on the stage at the time.

Speaking in protest over the absence of Ziaur Rahman’s photograph from the banner, district BNP joint convener MA Wahab said fascism had been ousted, but its collaborators remained in the administration.

They want to discredit the government’s development activities, he said. They believe fascism has persisted in Joypurhat as well. He expressed hope that the district administration would be more careful when organising such events in future.

Masud Rana Pradhan, administrator of the district council and a joint convener of the district BNP, said they were observing National Revolution and Solidarity Day after 19 years. Yet the banner at an event organised centering martyred President Ziaur Rahman, did not even feature his photograph.

In his speech as chief guest, State Minister Abdul Bari expressed anger over various shortcomings in the event. He said that if the incident had been intentional, action would certainly be taken. He instructed the deputy commissioner and the district council administrator to look into the matter.

The incident has deeply hurt party leaders and activists, he said, describing it as extremely painful. He drew State Minister Abdul Bari’s attention to the matter.

In his speech as chief guest, State Minister Abdul Bari expressed anger over various shortcomings in the event. He said that if the incident had been intentional, action would certainly be taken. He instructed the deputy commissioner and the district council administrator to look into the matter.

Deputy Commissioner Al-Mamun Mia apologised for the incident at the meeting. When asked about the absence of the photograph from the banner, he told Prothom Alo that it had been made using an image taken from the internet.

Among others, Superintendent of Police Shahnaz Begum, Civil Surgeon Al-Mamun, district BNP convener Golzar Hossain and district Muktijoddha Dal leader Jaglul Alam spoke at the meeting.

item.title: 35 senior govt officials to travel to Pakistan for training
item.description:
Under the development programme, 35 senior government officials from Bangladesh are going to Pakistan for training. Among them are five officials with the rank of Additional Secretary and 30 officials with the rank of Joint Secretary.

This 14-day training will be held at the National School of Public Policy in Lahore, Pakistan, starting from 9 November and ending on 22 November. A government order (GO) concerning the training of senior officials was issued by the Ministry of Public Administration last Wednesday.

Previously, in May, 12 senior officials from Bangladesh visited Pakistan for training for the first time. They received training at the Civil Services Academy (CSA) in Lahore, Pakistan, from 4 May to 21 May. Among the participants were one official with the rank of Additional Secretary and 11 with the rank of Joint Secretary.

In this second phase of advanced training, 35 officials are going to Lahore, including four officials from the Ministry of Public Administration, two each from the Cabinet Division and the Prime Minister's Office, and the rest from various ministries. They are scheduled to leave Dhaka on 8 November. After receiving a letter from the Ministry of Public Administration, the names of officials for training were selected by various ministries.

According to the government order issued by the Ministry of Public Administration, all expenses related to travel, accommodation, and training of the officials will be borne by the Pakistani government. There is no financial involvement of the Bangladesh government in this tour. Participants must submit a report within five working days of returning to the country at the end of the training.

Mustafa Zaman, Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Public Administration, who is at the top of the list, told Prothom Alo that at the invitation of the Pakistani government, this 14-day training will teach how the country's administration and development activities are conducted. Additionally, training will be provided on good governance, human resource management, and government policy strategies.

Training programme in India halted: According to sources in the Ministry of Public Administration, for a long time, Mussoorie in India was one of the primary foreign training destinations for Bangladeshi government officials.

Mid-level officials from Bangladesh regularly attended training at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration located in Mussoorie, Uttarakhand. This training programme started during the Awami League government when a memorandum of understanding was signed with the Delhi-based National Centre for Good Governance (NCGG) in 2014.

A second agreement was made between the two countries on 9 February 2019, and a third on 30 April 2024, in Dhaka. The last agreement was for one year, and there had been discussions about extending it until 2030.

According to sources from the Ministry of Public Administration, there was a diplomatic strain between Dhaka and Delhi after the fall of the Awami League government following the student-mass uprising on 5 August 2024. Since then, Bangladeshi government officials have not been sent to India for training. The training programme is suspended due to political change, diplomatic friction, the expiration of agreements, and visa complications. Instead, senior officials are now being sent to Pakistan for training.

Officials believe that training is required in both India and Pakistan. They opine that overseas training enhances bilateral cooperation, provides a platform for exchanging administrative experiences, and fosters leadership development. Maintaining a balance in relations with both countries is crucial, given the geopolitical realities of South Asia.

Relevant sources from the Ministry of Public Administration stated that the Pakistani government, at various times, invited Bangladesh for training through letters, but these invitations were not responded to during the Awami League government. The topic arose again when the then Home Secretary and now Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani visited Pakistan under the interim government.

When Pakistan proposed sending Bangladeshi officials for training, a positive response was given. After the BNP formed the government in the 13th national parliamentary elections, the Pakistani government formally sent an invitation through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh. It is essentially based on this invitation that officials are being sent to Pakistan.

An official from the Ministry of Public Administration told Prothom Alo that there has been no formal agreement between Bangladesh and Pakistan regarding the training yet. To establish an understanding and mutual acquaintance between the officials of both countries, officials are being sent for now, and an agreement will be reached subsequently. According to government sources, as part of the administrative capacity development programme, government officials are visiting Pakistan for this training.

Public administration analysts say that the initiative to send government officials for training to Pakistan also carries a diplomatic message amidst the political realities of South Asia. They suggest that government officials should be sent to multiple countries for training instead of relying on a single country.

item.title: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman joins BNP procession from Naya Paltan
item.description:
A procession organised by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) to mark the historic 7 November National Revolution and Solidarity Day has begun from Naya Paltan.

The procession started at around 3pm on Saturday in front of the party’s central office in Naya Paltan, Dhaka. Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman has joined the procession.

Tarique Rahman joined shortly after the procession began. He is walking at the front of the procession, which is moving from Naya Paltan towards Manik Mia Avenue.

BNP central leaders and activists of the party’s affiliated and associate organisations are also taking part.

According to the BNP’s programme, the procession started from Naya Paltan and turned right near the Chief Justice’s residence. It passed in front of the InterContinental Hotel, and proceed through Banglamotor and Farmgate. The procession ends at Manik Mia Avenue.

BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi announced the procession at a press conference at the party’s central office in Naya Paltan on Friday.

The BNP is observing a seven-day programme to mark National Revolution and Solidarity Day. The programme began last Thursday and includes discussion meetings, a procession and a photo exhibition.

item.title: What happened on 7 November and what I saw
item.description:
7 November 1975, was one of the most decisive turning points in Bangladesh’s political history. As a military officer, Brigadier General (Retd.) M Sakhawat Hossain witnessed the various military activities and internal conflicts of the time from very close quarters. The following is a brief account of the events of November 7, excerpted from his book Roktakto Dinguli: 1975–1981 (The Bloody Days: 1975–1981), presented for the readers of Prothom Alo

7 November 1975. It was around midnight. I was awakened by the sounds of gunfire and cries of “Zindabad” (Long Live!) all around. Startled, I jumped out of bed. Everyone in the house was terrified. I went and stood on the back veranda, from where the main road of the cantonment was visible. There were numerous vehicles filled with soldiers. They were the ones making all the noise. As they continued moving forward, I saw several tanks speeding southward at full throttle.

Tracer rounds fired from anti-aircraft guns in the direction of Tejgaon Airport were turning the southern sky crimson. I could not understand what had suddenly happened. I remembered the leaflets distributed that evening and the rumours I had heard.

For a moment, I thought that perhaps fighting had broken out between the units involved in the 15 August coup and those supporting Khaled Mosharraf. If that was indeed the case, then the civil war that had been feared over the past few days in this newly independent country might have just begun.

On the floor below mine lived Lieutenant Colonel Mashahad Chowdhury, commander of the anti-aircraft unit, one battery of which had been stationed at Tejgaon Airport to block access to the airport. They called us downstairs and took us into their living room. He then told me a great deal about what was happening. He explained how one battery of his unit had been taken to the airport and deployed without his orders. He also told me many things about the leaflets circulated the previous day.

Even then, we could not quite grasp what was actually unfolding outside. By the time I finished talking with him, it was almost morning. The sounds of gunfire continued throughout the night. Amid it all, the call to prayer could be heard.

As the eastern sky began to grow somewhat brighter, I quickly put on my uniform and decided to walk towards Brigade Headquarters with my neighbour, Major Harun (later Colonel, retired). Since Harun was serving as a staff officer at Station Headquarters, he too decided to walk there. So the two of us set out together.

As soon as we reached the main road, we came across two officers we knew. One was Major Mashuk Ahmed Chowdhury (later Brigadier, now retired), and the other was Lieutenant Colonel Sharif, a director in the Adjutant General’s Branch at Army Headquarters. He was a batchmate of both Shafiullah and Zia. The two were riding the same motorcycle. Mashuk was in uniform, while Lieutenant Colonel Sharif was still wearing the clothes he had on during the night.

Seeing us, they said that General Ziaur Rahman had just been released from captivity and taken to the 2 Field Regiment. They told us to go there, adding that other officers were also present. They had no time to say anything more, and we could barely hear them over the surrounding noise.

A military truck packed with soldiers and a number of civilian youths sped past us from the opposite direction, firing shots and chanting slogans. I had never heard these slogans before. The moment I heard them, my blood ran cold. They were chanting:

“Sepoys and sepoys, brothers all, We want the officers’ blood!”

“Long live the Sepoy Revolution! Long live General Zia!”

After hearing these slogans, Harun and I quickened our pace. Two more trucks sped past us along the way. Sitting atop them were military personnel accompanied by several armed civilian youths. I later learned that these civilian youths were members of the Gono Bahini, trained by Colonel Taher. Even then, I had no idea whose revolution this was or what kind of revolution was underway.

I also noticed one or two young officers among these revolutionary soldiers. They had no rank insignia on their shoulders. When I called one of them over and asked him about it, he replied: “Sir, from today onward, there will be no distinction in rank between sepoys and officers. There will be no hierarchy in the armed forces. That is the central principle of this revolution.”

I was utterly stunned. Could it be that Colonel Taher’s Biplobi Sainik Sangstha (Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation) had staged the revolution? Was this perhaps the beginning of Taher’s class struggle and an initial attempt to seize state power as the first step towards achieving it?

Several more jeeps sped past us. By then, there was little left to doubt. Members of the JSD’s Gono Bahini, who had been trained for class struggle, were now inside the cantonment alongside the soldiers.

We walked quickly and reached the main gate of the Second Field Regiment. The first person I met there was the unit’s Subedar Major Anis (later Honorary Captain). As soon as he saw me, Anis embraced me and said, “Sir, by the grace of Allah, we have found you. There is nobody at the brigade. No one can be found anywhere. Zia shaheb is looking for you all.”

He briefly explained that after the “Sepoy Revolution” began around midnight, the guards from the First Bengal Regiment had been removed. In the morning, Major Mohiuddin (later Lieutenant Colonel), along with other soldiers from this very regiment, had brought Zia to their unit. At that moment, Zia was in the commanding officer’s office. Several other officers were with him, as was Brigadier Mir Shawkat Ali, commander of the 55 Brigade in Jessore.

That day, the Second Field Regiment became the centre of power in Bangladesh—not merely within the armed forces, but in the country as a whole. It is worth remembering that the Second Field Regiment was one of the two units that participated in the August 15 coup under Rashid’s leadership.

When we arrived at the Second Field Regiment, I found only about 10 to 15 officers there. The scenes unfolding there from one moment to the next gave me the impression that the army had never existed as an institution in Bangladesh. It seemed that no one had any authority there, nor had anyone ever exercised any.

In the unit quarter guard, where military prisoners were held, I saw several familiar officers confined in the cells. Among them was Lieutenant Colonel Bahar. I could never have imagined witnessing a senior freedom fighter officer being held in a quarter guard cell in this manner. It was an unprecedented sight.

When I asked Subedar Major Anis about the circumstances, the gist of his explanation was that the revolutionary soldiers, angered by the conduct of certain officers, had drawn up a list of their names. They then went from house to house, attacking them. Upon hearing of these attacks, the frightened officers began fleeing, leaving their families behind. Those who were found were brought into protective custody to save their lives from attacks by the frenzied soldiers.

Subedar Major Anis could not say exactly who had ordered that these officers be taken into this protective custody. However, regarding Lieutenant Colonel Bahar, he explained that Bahar had actively participated in the operation against Zia in his capacity as commander of Army Signals and had grievances on other matters as well. When the revolutionary soldiers began pursuing him, Bahar himself had asked Anis to shelter him in the quarter guard.

Having grasped the underlying significance of Anis's account, I made my way calmly into the commanding officer's office. As I entered, I saw Major General Ziaur Rahman seated in the commanding officer's chair. Beside him was Brigadier Mir Shawkat Ali, dressed in a safari suit.

After entering, I saluted Zia. He told me, “Go to the brigade. Take control of the soldiers there. I spoke to your commander (Shafayat Jamil) a little while ago; he is doing well. Amin has been appointed the new commander.”

As I left the office after hearing what he had to say, I ran into AJM. Aminul Haque. He advised me to remain there for some time, observe everything, and assess the situation before proceeding to the brigade. He further explained that, since none of the other brigade staff officers could be found and he himself was new to the position, he could not leave his unit, the Fourth Bengal, under the circumstances. Therefore, I would have to take charge of all the responsibilities on my own.

When he asked me to take over the duties of BM (Brigade Major) in place of Hafiz, I assured him that I would look after things there. He also informed me that neither Brigade Major Hafiz nor Staff Captain Taj could be found anywhere in the cantonment.

As soon as Ziaur Rahman arrived at the Second Field Regiment, he asked for Khaled Mosharraf at Bangabhaban. However, unable to find him, he managed to get in touch with Shafayat Jamil instead. As soon as news of the Sepoy Revolution reached them, Khaled Mosharraf, Huda and Haider had left Bangabhaban together. Consequently, Zia eventually contacted Shafayat Jamil.

When Ziaur Rahman met Shafayat Jamil, he told him, “Forget and forgive. You come back.”

In response, Shafayat Jamil said something along the lines of, “I am a rebel and will remain so.”

Shafayat Jamil has himself recorded in his book what else he told Ziaur Rahman. He writes, “You cannot stage a revolt through the soldiers and expect to remain in power. You have mounted a tiger's back, and you will not be able to get off. Whatever you wanted to do, you could have done it with the officers. Why involve the soldiers?”

He also expressed his deep resentment over the introduction of a politics of hatred and division within the army.

He further stated that someone had been eavesdropping on his conversation with Zia and translating it into English. Shafayat had overheard the translation because of a crossed telephone connection. At the time, while Shafayat Jamil was speaking to Zia from inside Bangabhaban, he may not have realised that the force behind the coup was not Zia but Taher, his “Gono Bahini” (People’s Army), and the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation—at least at that stage of events.

When Shafayat Jamil was informed around midnight about the revolution that had taken place inside the cantonment, he still had no clear understanding of the actual situation. By the time he learned what was really happening, it was already too late. After Khaled Mosharraf left Bangabhaban, Shafayat Jamil realised that he was the only one left behind there.

At around the early hours of dawn, he received a telephone call from Ziaur Rahman and learned that some revolutionary soldiers had arrived at the main gate of Bangabhaban looking for them. Deeply alarmed, he handed the car keys to the driver and attempted to escape by climbing over the rear wall of Bangabhaban. In doing so, he broke one of his legs.

He and Major Didar Ataur, the Fourth Bengal company commander stationed at Bangabhaban, travelled together in a car along the Dhaka–Chittagong Highway as far as the Meghna ferry terminal. By then, Shafayat Jamil could no longer continue because of his broken leg.

As fate would have it, they encountered the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) of Narayanganj there (Narayanganj was a subdivision at the time). The SDO was about to depart for Narayanganj by launch. Didar Ataur and Shafayat Jamil introduced themselves and explained that Jamil urgently needed medical attention. The SDO then took them aboard his launch.

After Shafayat Jamil received initial medical treatment, the SDO handed him and his companion over to the Bandar Police Station. It was from there that, on the morning of November 7, Shafayat Jamil spoke to General Ziaur Rahman over the telephone. A few days later, he was admitted to CMH (Combined Military Hospital) for specialised medical treatment. Until the last day of his life, he walked with a slight limp because of his broken leg.

Standing on the veranda of the Second Field Regiment, I saw Colonel Taher enter Ziaur Rahman’s room, surrounded by several soldiers and members of the Gono Bahini. Among his companions were also a few members of the Second Field Regiment. Initially, Taher and Zia embraced. As soon as the embrace ended, Taher asked Ziaur Rahman to go to the radio station and address the nation.

However, even before Taher arrived, Ziaur Rahman, while seated at the Second Field Regiment, had already recorded his address on the advice of other officers and sent the recording to the radio station for broadcast.

Later, Taher presented Zia with a list of demands on behalf of the soldiers. Zia said he would consider the matter at a later time and kept the list. Taher was evidently not particularly pleased with Zia’s response. After speaking privately with Zia for a while, he left the office in an agitated state.

Although the details of what Taher and Zia discussed that day are not known, some information was available from unverified sources. However, from the very beginning of the Sepoy Revolution, Radio Bangladesh (the renamed Bangladesh Betar) remained under the control of the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation and the JSD’s Gono Bahini for an extended period. Zia was prevented from going there in person to deliver his address.

This was done because Taher had wanted from the very beginning to use Zia entirely to serve his own political objectives. Taher wanted to take Zia to the radio station so that he could announce the soldiers’ demands and declare what the future structure or political framework of the state would look like.

According to further accounts from various unverified sources, Taher’s plan was to take Zia from the radio station to the Shaheed Minar and have him address the members of the Gono Bahini and the revolutionary soldiers there. The revolutionary soldiers allegedly planned to shoot and kill Zia on his way back. During the brief period when Mir Shawkat Ali served as Chief of General Staff (CGS), he had reportedly made statements to this effect.

The following day, November 8, Ziaur Rahman returned to Army Headquarters in his capacity as Chief of Army Staff. Brigadier Mir Shawkat Ali was appointed CGS in place of Khaled Mosharraf.

That very morning, I heard that four officers had been killed by the soldiers.

Among them, a female doctor named Hamida and a dental surgeon named Karim were killed purely out of personal animosity. Two other officers, who were undergoing training at the Bangladesh hockey camp—Captain Anwar and Lieutenant Mostafiz—were chased towards the television station and killed there.

The ordinary soldiers who had spontaneously joined the so-called Sepoy-People’s Revolution of 7 November were also beginning to become disillusioned. Gradually, rank-and-file soldiers began distancing themselves from the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation. Those who had chanted “Sepoys and sepoys, brothers all” on November 7 and 8 were increasingly becoming directionless in the absence of effective leadership.

It is worth noting that most members of the killer group Colonel Taher had formed within the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation were soldiers from various service corps of the army and the Air Force. Dhaka had four infantry battalions under the 46 Brigade. Apart from the battalion stationed at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, another newly formed battalion also refrained from joining the activities of the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation on 7 and 8 November.

Had Taher’s plan succeeded, the army’s command structure would have collapsed that very night or within the following few days, and Ziaur Rahman would have been assassinated before state power was seized.

Under these circumstances, Zia began to realise that Taher had been defeated this time. Gradually, almost the entire armed forces—including commanders, officers and soldiers both inside and outside Dhaka—began looking to Zia for leadership and direction. Overall, the country was passing through an extremely precarious situation.

Beginning on 8 November, Ziaur Rahman wasted no time. Moving almost at breakneck speed, he toured the entire cantonment, meeting and speaking with soldiers. At various gatherings, he repeatedly emphasised the need to restore the army's chain of command. Later that afternoon, he summoned the soldiers of Dhaka Cantonment near the Fourth Bengal Regiment's barracks and spoke to them.

Remarkably, on that day, there were only about 40 to 50 officers in the entire Dhaka Cantonment. Apart from those 40 to 50 officers, everyone else in the cantonment was armed.

In a firm voice, Ziaur Rahman ordered the soldiers to surrender their weapons and return to their respective barracks. He further announced that he would accept their legitimate demands and that, after giving the matter due consideration as soon as possible, he would inform them of his decisions at the appropriate time. He made this announcement on behalf of the government, although Justice Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem had, at that point, been asked to continue serving as President.

While Zia was speaking at the gathering about restoring discipline among the soldiers and surrendering their weapons, one soldier accidentally shot and killed himself with his own rifle. Following Zia’s speech, the soldiers agreed to surrender their weapons.

Later that afternoon, when the weapons were being surrendered, a number of soldiers who were ardent admirers of Colonel (Retd.) Taher and staunch followers of his Soldiers’ Organisation began spreading inflammatory propaganda against Zia. That evening, some members of the organisation dragged three innocent officers out of the Ordnance Mess and killed them right in front of the mess.

It was 8 November. At around 9 pm, I was sitting at Brigade Headquarters when a signal operator from the brigade came and informed me that the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation had once again drawn up a list of several officers marked for elimination that night.

The essence of what he reported was this: unless all the soldiers’ demands were met, the struggle would continue. He further informed me that only a handful of soldiers were involved in the killing of officers, particularly some members of the Signals, Lancers and military clerical corps who supported the soldiers organisation. The activities of the Revolutionary Soldiers’ Organisation were largely concentrated among these groups.

Had Taher’s plan succeeded, the army’s command structure would have collapsed that very night or within the following few days, and Ziaur Rahman would have been assassinated before state power was seized. Taher had won over ordinary soldiers by promising to secure their various demands. He would cite examples of what he described as the feudalistic behaviour and practices of military officers to his supporters.

It appears that, after dismantling the army’s structure through such propaganda, as they had planned, they would have launched similar attacks on the civilian bureaucracy. This would have plunged the country into a state of extreme chaos, putting its sovereignty and independence at risk.

In fact, Taher was an exceptionally self-confident and highly ambitious man. As soon as Ziaur Rahman understood the extent of Taher’s ambitions, he began distancing himself from him and swiftly took steps to bring the soldiers back under discipline. Owing to Ziaur Rahman’s popularity, personality, courage and prompt decision-making, the entire situation came under his control within a day or two.

* Brigadier General (Retd.) M Sakhawat Hossain is a former adviser to the caretaker government. He served as an Election Commissioner from 2007 to 2012.

item.title: Hridoy makes history with maiden Test double century
item.description:
CRICKET-BAN-WIS-TEST

Tawhid Hridoy became the first Bangladesh batter to score a double century in his maiden Test hundred, producing a remarkable innings to lead the hosts' fightback against West Indies in the second Test in Sylhet.

Bangladesh reached 340 for eight in 101 overs in their first innings, just 16 runs behind West Indies' total of 356, with Hridoy unbeaten on 200.

The right-handed batter reached the milestone off 304 balls, hitting 19 fours and seven sixes.

He brought up his double century with a single off Jomel Warrican after tea on the third day.

Hridoy is now the fourth Bangladesh batter to score a double century in Test cricket, joining Mushfiqur Rahim, Tamim Iqbal and Shakib Al Hasan.

What makes his achievement particularly remarkable is that he scored most of his runs while batting with the lower-order players.

After the dismissal of Mehidy Hasan Miraz, the last recognised batter, Hridoy added 131 runs to his total while keeping Bangladesh in the contest.

Earlier, Hridoy had surpassed Mominul Haque's 181 against New Zealand in Chattogram in 2013 to become the highest-scoring Bangladesh batter in his maiden Test century.

His innings also helped Bangladesh recover from 205 for seven at lunch, putting the hosts in a strong position to challenge West Indies' first-innings total.

item.title: PM calls for unity to prevent rights violations, foreign domination
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday called for national unity to ensure that no one can again deprive people of their rights or turn Bangladesh into a subservient state.
“Let this be our main pledge on this November 7 that no one will ever again be able to take away the rights of the country and its people or turn Bangladesh into a subservient state,” he said.
Addressing a special display programme at the Army Stadium in the capital's Banani, marking the National Revolution and Solidarity Day, the prime minister said national unity was essential to fulfil this pledge.
He said the spirit of the November 7 revolution of soldiers and people must be upheld to maintain national unity, considering Bangladesh's socioeconomic, geographical and political realities.
Referring to the November 7 revolution of 1975 and anti-autocracy movement of 1990 and the mass uprising against fascism in 2024, Tarique said the country's youth had proved through every historic event that they never compromised on the question of Bangladesh's interests.
He said achieving independence was a matter of historic pride, but preserving its honour and making it meaningful was the responsibility of every generation, particularly the younger generation.
“The responsibility of the young generation is to uphold the spirit of independence and devote themselves to building a safe, prosperous, humane and dignified Bangladesh,” the prime minister said.
He said the responsibility of guardians was to ensure an appropriate environment for young people to develop their full potential.
