item.title: Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: The growing threat of unclean air
item.description:
Dhaka's air pollution has once again reached alarming levels, with the capital recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 203 on Friday morning. Classified as “very unhealthy,” this reading is another reminder of a public health crisis that continues to receive far less attention than it deserves.
Air pollution is not a seasonal inconvenience that residents should simply learn to live with. It is a serious threat to public health, contributing to respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, and other long-term complications. Children, older people, and those with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable, but the consequences extend to everyone who breathes the city's air.
The sources of this pollution are well known: Unregulated construction, road dust, emissions from ageing vehicles, industrial pollution, and brick kilns all contribute to the problem. Yet, despite repeated warnings and directives, meaningful improvements remain difficult to see.
The courts have previously issued directives to tackle air pollution, including controlling construction dust and shutting down illegal brick kilns. The continued deterioration of air quality raises serious questions about how effectively these measures are being enforced.
We need more than occasional drives and temporary interventions. Authorities must coordinate their efforts, enforce environmental regulations and hold those responsible for pollution accountable.
Construction sites must follow dust-control requirements, illegal brick kilns must be shut down, and vehicle emissions must be monitored more strictly. Regular monitoring and transparent reporting should also become standard practice.
At the same time, improving public transport, expanding green spaces, and investing in sustainable urban planning must be treated as long-term priorities.
People should not have to choose between going outside and protecting their health.
Let us be clear: Clean air is a basic necessity, not a privilege. Dhaka's worsening pollution demands urgent, sustained action. Another day of alarming AQI readings should not remain another day of inaction.

item.title: Men neither see nor listen to women
item.description:
Searching the Dhaka Tribune last week for a piece of my own, I came instead upon an essay I have not been able to put down: Shuchi binte Shahjalal’s The women are divine .
She opens with the old belief of the idol-makers: That a Durga is incomplete unless a little earth from a sex worker’s doorstep is worked into her clay -- for a man leaves his virtue at that threshold, and the ground there turns holy. The goddess cannot be finished without the woman’s soil; the woman herself cannot be let into the festival. The earth is holy, she writes. The person is not.
Let me say at once what I am and am not doing. I am a man, and this is a piece about men. I will not presume to explain to the women of my homeland a cage they have mapped, from the inside, far better than I can.
Shuchi has already said the essential thing, with a scholar’s range and a poet’s aim. I want only to add a footnote -- from the poet we Bengalis reach for whenever we wish to sound reverent about women, and whom, I have come to think, we never actually heard.
We are fond of Tagore as a worshipper of the feminine. We quote him at weddings and drape our daughters’ recitals in his songs. It is worth remembering, then, that at his most attentive, the Bishwakobi was not building the pedestal Shuchi describes. He was warning against it.
I have spent this autumn translating his love songs, one line at a time, and two of them will not now leave me.
The first is Bhalobeshe, sokhi, nibhrite jatone -- “Love me, and in the quiet shrine of your heart, write my name.” Midway, the lover makes a stranger, smaller request:
“Keep, with tender care, my chattering bird, in the courtyard of your palace.”
Read it slowly, and the bird is no ornament. The whole ache of the song is the plea that it be kept, tended, listened to.
In a second song, Tumi ki keboli chhobi -- “Are you only a picture?” -- he almost begs her not to harden into mere paint on a canvas, to be real and present, not an image he can hang on a wall and admire.
A century before our present arguments, Tagore had already named the two ways a man fails a woman: He stops listening to her voice, and he lets her freeze into an image.
Shuchi calls on Nazrul, who dared to address the barangana , the prostitute, as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her.
Let me call on the other giant, who stands, I think, exactly where she does -- on the side of the woman no one will look at or listen to.
Her essay is unsparing about what reverence costs, in life and in death. She recalls the roughly 1,500 women driven from the Kandapara brothel in Tangail in 2014, long after a High Court had ruled such evictions unconstitutional; the sex workers ridiculed when they report rape, because the society “cannot imagine a sex worker being raped”; and Hamida Begum, who in 2020 became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a proper Islamic burial -- after which the imam who prayed over her said he would not do it again, having been scolded by his neighbours.
Beside these, she sets the national figures she cites: By the counts of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, 786 women and girls raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before; and almost 22,000 cases of violence against women and children logged by police in a single year.
I will not borrow her numbers to decorate an argument of my own. I note only what she notices -- that behind each is a woman whom a society that sorts its women into goddesses and fallen women has filed under the second heading.
And I would underline, for every man who thinks himself devout, the sentence of hers that ought to be read aloud from pulpits: A society that calls its women mothers and then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist walks, has not forgotten reverence -- it has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
Here, let me add the one thing a lifetime in medicine has taught me, because it bears on her point that rape is treated as a stain on a woman’s honour rather than a crime against her body.
I have spent my working life with the human heart -- the actual muscle, four chambers, no holier in a saint than in a so-called fallen woman. A body keeps no ledger of honour. It bleeds the same, grieves the same, heals or fails to heal the same, whatever box the neighbours have assigned its owner.
When we treat a woman’s injury as a stain on her family’s ijjat rather than harm to her person, we are not being moral. We are staring at the honour and refusing to see the woman -- the same failure, once more.
So the answer, I think, is not less reverence but reverence that finally opens its eyes. Read generously, the idol-maker’s belief is almost holy: The goddess is made, in part, of the outcast woman’s earth; the divine and the discarded are the same clay.
The tragedy is only that we stop at the clay. We bow to the figure and walk past the person who gave it her soil.
Tagore points where Shuchi points. Keep the chattering bird -- do not cage it, do not silence it, bend down and listen. Do not let her become only a picture on the wall.
The cure for a goddess no one can bear to meet is not to break her into a “fallen” woman; it is to come down off our own certainty and stand beside her at the doorstep -- to see her face, and to hear her voice.
Shuchi binte Shahjalal has written the diagnosis. The least her countrymen -- and I mean the men -- can do is read it with our eyes open for once, and admit what it took a woman on the Op-Ed desk to say plainly.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, many still hiding their faces: Divine in theory, and in practice neither seen nor heard.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, where he practises medicine.

item.title: We need more public-private partnership
item.description:
A healthcare system under unrealistic pressure like ours needs practical ways to improve the quality and reach of public hospitals, and this initiative, if implemented carefully, could address some of the gaps that have long undermined public healthcare.
Under the proposed pilot, private partners will provide services at five tertiary-level hospitals, with fees still to be finalized before the program begins.
The intention to expand the model to other cities is also encouraging. Public hospitals face shortages of equipment, specialized services, and trained personnel. Private expertise and investment could improve facilities, strengthen management, and give patients access to treatment that might otherwise be out of reach.
However, this partnership must strengthen public healthcare, not make essential treatment a privilege. Fees charged by private partners need to be reasonable and clearly disclosed. Patients should not face unexpected costs, and those unable to afford additional charges must not be pushed aside.
The government must set firm standards for service quality, monitor performance, and hold partners accountable for meeting agreed targets.
The initiative must also complement sustained public investment. Bangladesh cannot rely on private participation alone to resolve long standing weaknesses in healthcare.
Hospitals need adequate staffing, functioning equipment, regular maintenance and better management. Plans to recruit more doctors and expand critical care facilities must move forward without unnecessary delays.
The five-hospital pilot should be an opportunity to measure results and correct shortcomings before expansion. The government must publish clear information on costs, services and outcomes so the public can judge whether the program is working.
This is precisely the kind of practical initiative the health sector needs more of. With transparency, affordability, and proper oversight, partnerships can help deliver better care to more people.
The real test, however, will be whether patients experience meaningful improvements.

item.title: Rizvi: Nov 7 gave Bangladesh new direction
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Saturday said November 7, 1975 revolution and solidarity movement gave Bangladesh a new direction and renewed hope for independence, sovereignty and multiparty democracy.
Nov 7 movement carried three commitments, protecting independence, safeguarding sovereignty and ensuring the continuation of multiparty democracy, and that people took to the streets in July, 2024 with those ideals to defeat what he described as anti-democratic force, he told reporters after paying tributes marking the 51st anniversary of the National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman paid tribute to Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia at their graves at 8:30am on behalf of the BNP, marking the day.
He said the spirit of November 7 had repeatedly inspired the people of Bangladesh to stand up for freedom, democracy and national sovereignty.
Referring to the political developments of 1975, Rizvi said the country was plunged into anarchy following the events of January 25, when the one-party BAKSAL system was introduced, curtailing people's civil rights.
He said the nation was subsequently pushed into a period of uncertainty and bloodshed, while Ziaur Rahman and his family were detained at their cantonment residence ahead of November 7.
According to Rizvi, people were then deeply concerned about the restoration of BAKSAL, the loss of civil liberties and restrictions on the press.
Rizvi said now some quarters are attempting to disrupt the country's democratic journey by creating instability.
"Sometimes you see crude bombs and cocktails being exploded inside alleys. Instructions are reportedly coming from a neighbouring country while people acting as hired killers and receiving money are trying in various ways to disrupt Bangladesh's democratic journey," he said.
Rizvi said the people would appropriately resist such attempts.
He also warned that the public is observing the activities of different political parties and those trying to take advantage of the situation by creating confusion.
He said people would not forgive anyone who attempted to mislead them or obstruct the democratic process.
Rizvi said the BNP and its supporters remained committed to resisting all undemocratic and anti-national forces, drawing inspiration from the spirit of the Revolution and Solidarity Day.
He said the party would work alongside the people to protect their civil liberties and maintain the continuity of the country's development and production.

item.title: World Bank approves $300m loan to improve primary education
item.description:
The World Bank has approved a $300 million loan to Bangladesh to improve the quality of primary education and address learning gaps among children.
The funding will support programmes aimed at improving education for 26 million children, from pre-primary to Grade 5. The initiatives will focus on strengthening foundational reading, writing and mathematics skills, while providing targeted support to students who are falling behind.
The World Bank’s Board of Executive Directors approved the financing in Washington, DC, on Friday under a programme titled Learning Enhancement and Acceleration in Primary Education (LEAP).
According to a World Bank press release, the financing will support the implementation of Bangladesh’s Fifth Primary Education Development Programme. The initiative will focus on improving pre-primary and primary education, training teachers and strengthening school management.
Although Bangladesh has achieved near-universal access to primary education, learning outcomes remain a major challenge. World Bank data show that around 50% of 10-year-old children in the country cannot read and understand a simple text appropriate for their age and grade level. The comparable figures are 42% in Malaysia, an upper-middle-income country, and 47% in Brazil.
Jean Pesme, World Bank country director for Bangladesh and Bhutan, said quality primary education was essential to building a workforce capable of competing globally.
Over the past two decades, the World Bank has supported Bangladesh in expanding access to schooling, helping ensure that nearly all children have the opportunity to attend school, he said. The new financing would help children learn more effectively and stay in school, improving their future employment prospects.
The World Bank described Bangladesh’s primary education system as one of the largest in the world, with more than 20 million students enrolled across government primary schools, private and NGO-run schools, kindergartens and madrasas.
Under the programme, a specialized learning package will be introduced to strengthen foundational literacy and numeracy. It will include teaching materials, structured lesson plans and teacher training.
Headteachers from 90% of government primary schools will also receive training in leadership and management, while school governance and management systems will be strengthened.
Students who fall behind will receive remedial education and supplementary instruction, with particular attention given to districts where learning gaps are most severe.
Tasmina Rahman, a senior education specialist at the World Bank and the programme’s team leader, said strengthening foundational learning was the first step towards developing the skills needed for quality employment.
The programme would provide targeted support to ensure no child was left behind, while improving teaching quality and school leadership, strengthening accountability for the use of funds and increasing the use of data in decision-making, she said.
Teachers in government primary schools will receive training and support to teach reading, writing and mathematics more effectively. The programme will also seek to improve pre-primary education in government primary schools to better prepare children for formal schooling.
The World Bank expects the programme to create 843,000 new, relatively well-paid job opportunities within the government primary school system.
The financing is being provided by the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA), which offers concessional loans and grants to low-income countries.
The loan has a 25-year maturity period, including a five-year grace period during which no repayments will be required.

item.title: Dhaka’s air quality 4th worst in the world Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the overcrowded capital city of Bangladesh, has ranked 4th on the list of cities with the worst air quality with an AQI index of 189 at 9:08am on Saturday.
Dhaka’s air was classified as "unhealthy", according to the air quality and pollution city ranking.
India’s Delhi, Pakistan’s Lahore and India's Kolkata occupied the first, second and third spots in the list, with AQI scores of 539, 273 and 198, respectively.
When the AQI value for particle pollution is between 101 and 150, air quality is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", between 150 and 200 is "unhealthy", between 201 and 300 is said to be "very unhealthy", while a reading of 301+ is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
The AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, informs people how clean or polluted the air of a certain city is and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
The AQI in Bangladesh is based on five pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2, and ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.

item.title: Hridoy's maiden Test century keeps Bangladesh afloat in Sylhet
item.description:
Towhid Hridoy struck his maiden Test century as wickets fell around him, taking Bangladesh to 205 for seven at lunch on the third day of the second Test against West Indies in Sylhet on Saturday.
Hridoy reached his hundred just before the break and was unbeaten on 100 off 171 balls, with 11 fours and a six. Bangladesh still trail West Indies' first-innings 356 by 151 runs.
With opener Shadman Islam unable to bat in the first innings because of an ankle injury, Bangladesh have only Taijul Islam and Taskin Ahmed left to support Hridoy.
Bangladesh resumed on 88 for three and added 117 runs in the morning session, losing four wickets, three of them to West Indies' spinners.
Hridoy and Mushfiqur Rahim took their fourth-wicket stand to 78 before left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican struck. Mushfiqur drove a flighted delivery from around the wicket straight to Brandon King at short cover, who dived to his left to take the catch. Mushfiqur made 34, and Bangladesh were 129 for four.
Hridoy reached his first Test fifty off 109 balls in the next over. Liton Das then fell the same way as Mushfiqur, driving Warrican to King at cover for eight, leaving Bangladesh on 141 for five.
Mehidy Hasan Miraz made 16 off 30 balls before Roston Chase had him caught by Justin Greaves, who dived to his right at first slip as Miraz attempted a paddle sweep. Bangladesh were 179 for six.
Warrican then removed Hasan Mahmud for one off 12 balls, caught behind on review after replays confirmed an outside edge, with Bangladesh on 184 for seven.
Hridoy and Taijul added an unbroken 21, with Hridoy scoring most of the runs. He celebrated his century by placing his helmet on the handle of his bat and raising it. Taijul was on one off 14 balls.
Warrican has taken three for 60.

item.title: Australia's Khawaja claims entire team knew about 'Sandpapergate'
item.description:
Former opener Usman Khawaja claimed on Saturday that the entire Australian team knew about the 2018 "Sandpapergate" scandal in Cape Town and said they also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth.
Captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were sent home in disgrace and found by a Cricket Australia investigation to be the only three players with prior knowledge of the ball-tampering plot.
Smith was banned for a year and sacked as skipper, Warner was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles while Bancroft was slapped with a nine-month ban.
But Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, told the Sydney Morning Herald everyone had prior knowledge.
"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," he said ahead of the release of his autobiography next week where a chapter is dedicated to the issue.
Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.
Khawaja said he spoke in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test urging the team to take collective responsibility, rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.
"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this." Khawaja said.
"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Maybe I thought Davey (Warner) would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn't think it was going to come down to this."
In the book, according to the newspaper, Khawaja recounts that discussions about ways to rough up the ball were also held in the dressing room during the second Test at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.
It culminated in the discovery that sandpaper was effective and at this point Smith allegedly walked away, saying he did not want to know about it.
Bancroft then allegedly volunteered to use sandpaper in South Africa's first innings in Gqeberha, where the ball swung significantly.
Cricket Australia said in a statement it was "comfortable" with the findings of its original investigation, but remained open to new evidence.
"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," it said.
"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.
"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

item.title: Alcaraz saves match points to reach Paris Masters semis
item.description:
Carlos Alcaraz produced another miracle in the French capital as the seven-time Grand Slam champion fended off two match points to beat Taylor Fritz and reach the Paris Masters semi-finals on Friday.
The 23-year-old fought back to win 6-7 (10/12), 7-5, 6-3 to advance to the last four of the event for the first time.
He will next take on former world number two Casper Ruud on Saturday after the Norwegian eliminated Portuguese lucky loser Nuno Borges 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
In scenes reminiscent of his iconic French Open final comeback win over Jannik Sinner last season, when he saved three championship points, Alcaraz again wowed the crowd in Paris as he snatched another improbable victory from the jaws of defeat.
"Probably this match is going to be one of the most special matches that I ever played, and I'm going to remember this match for a long time," Alcaraz told reporters.
Despite only playing one match en route to the quarter-finals, Alcaraz showed no signs of rust as he seized his first break opportunity in the fifth game of the opening set, whipping a forehand passing shot around the stranded Fritz.
The Spaniard's serve then started to wobble and Fritz pounced to break to love and level at 5-5.
In a tie-break of thrills and spills, both players had set points come and go before Alcaraz dumped a forehand wide to cede the opener to the Californian.
After recovering from 0-40 to hold early in the second set, Alcaraz pointed to his ear and held his fist aloft in a bid to get the Parisian crowd going -- the first but not last call-back to his five-set Roland Garros epic.
But he continued to struggle to make inroads on Fritz's serve and it was the American who produced the first break of the set in the seventh game.
Alcaraz staved off a match point and then secured a hold that kept his campaign alive with a sensational backhand slice from well wide of his own tramlines.
"After that game... I started to enjoy it because I just thought I pulled off great shots, great points, I started to smile, I started to bring the energy from the people to the match," the former world number one said.
A fine passing shot saved a second match point in the next game before Alcaraz wiped out the break and then completed his Houdini act by breaking Fritz again to set up a decider.
The rampant Murcian had a chokehold on the match and went in front 3-1 in the third set when Fritz pushed a volley wide.
Alcaraz still had to save break points in a match that always threatened another twist but, as it rumbled towards a conclusion, he brought up two match points on his own serve, sealing the first with a powerful forehand that Fritz could only get a frame on.
- Shelton advances -
Earlier, Ben Shelton edged Tommy Paul 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 in an all-American quarter-final.
The defeats for Paul and Fritz ended both players' hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals, with American Frances Tiafoe and Spanish 20-year-old Rafael Jodar now set to make their debuts at the season-ending showpiece, which will run from November 15-22 in Turin.
"Frances has had an outstanding year. One of my best friends, and to see him make Turin for the first time is amazing," Shelton said of the 28-year-old Finals debutant.
Shelton will meet Luca Van Assche in the last four after the Frenchman ended Australian Rinky Hijikata's fairytale run from qualifying to the last eight.

item.title: Mbappe headlines Zidane's France squad, Pagis gets call-up
item.description:
Kylian Mbappe headlined the France squad named Friday by coach Zinedine Zidane for their Nations League matches against Italy and Turkey after picking up an injury on international duty in September, while Pablo Pagis was handed a debut call-up.
Real Madrid superstar Mbappe, the France captain, scored the winner in Zidane's first match in charge of Les Bleus away to Turkey on September 25, but suffered a knee injury in the same game that ruled him out of the team's three remaining fixtures of the last international window.
Without him, France won twice against Belgium, in Brussels and then at home, and drew in between against Italy.
Mbappe has since returned to action for his club, scoring eight times in seven matches between La Liga and the Champions League.
France are without Paris Saint-Germain star Ousmane Dembele and Rennes striker Esteban Lepaul for this month's double-header, so Marcus Thuram of Inter Milan is recalled to an attack which will also feature Pagis for the first time.
The 23-year-old Pagis, who plays chiefly as an attacking midfielder, is rewarded for his impressive form this season since joining Paris FC -- who are fourth in Ligue 1 -- from Lorient.
Pagis is the son of Mickael Pagis, the former Marseille player who at one time appeared for the France beach soccer team coached by Eric Cantona.
Aurelien Tchouameni of Real Madrid returns in midfield in place of Manu Kone after missing the last international window, while Manchester United's Leny Yoro and Chelsea's Malo Gusto replace Jules Kounde of Barcelona and Maxence Lacroix of Chelsea in the defence.
Zidane's side play Italy in Milan next Thursday, November 12, and then take on Turkey in Bordeaux three days later in their final group-stage fixtures.
They are top of Nations League Group A1 with 10 points from four outings, three ahead of Italy.
The top two teams in the group will advance to the quarter-finals next March.

item.title: 'Enjoy the moment': The German clubs limiting smartphones in stadiums
item.description:
In October, Bundesliga club Borussia Dortmund did something not just out of step with modern football, but with modern life: they asked fans to put their phones away.
Ahead of last month's match with Eintracht Frankfurt, Dortmund launched a scheme which rewarded supporters for not using their smartphones during games at their 82,000-capacity Westfalenstadion.
By switching on 'fan mode' in the Dortmund app, supporters who kept off their phones were awarded points and could win prizes, including signed jerseys and fan shop vouchers.
But while the scheme likely seems odd, particularly for international fans, it has been warmly received in Germany, where the matchday experience remains sacred to millions of fans.
- 'Significant positive feedback' -
German football's unique governance rules -- which restrict external investment by requiring clubs to be member-owned -- have helped preserve the stadium experience lost elsewhere.
With fans playing a role in club decisions, preserving this experience remains paramount.
Season tickets at Bayern Munich, the defending German champions, start at 180 euros ($200) for 17 home Bundesliga games. By contrast, the cheapest season ticket for English champions Arsenal cost £978 ($1,309) for 19 home matches.
Dortmund are not the only club to try and curb in-game phone usage. Second division sides Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden also implemented restrictions this season.
The Hertha and Dynamo schemes have primarily sought to prevent the growing trend of influencers filming and monetising in-stadium content, but are also targeted at preserving the experience of being in the crowd.
Sporting organisations across the globe have grappled with what to do about influencers during major events. Some see it as a useful source of promotion, but others fear it detracts from the overall experience, while it can violate lucrative broadcast arrangements.
In response to dozens of incidents at the 2026 US Open tennis tournament, Wimbledon has decided to ban so-called content creators from 2027.
Hertha told AFP their scheme had tried to tackle the "fundamental question of how we deal with external video productions in our stadium".
Like Hertha, Dynamo said the policy was partially motivated by a need to protect broadcaster rights, but was also directed at preserving matchdays for everyone.
"The atmosphere and support of the team should be in the foreground for the stadium visit," Dynamo told AFP, while adding the project "received significant positive feedback from fans."
- 'Scream and stream' -
Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer said the policy preserves what makes the club special.
"It is a very unique approach. It's how to attract people, to tell them, 'hey, it's not a concert where you scream and stream video sequence by video sequence'," Cramer told AFP and other media.
"We should not avoid technological progress, but we should consider how to use it in our landscape, because the very emotional and authentic scenery of a football game has to be protected."
Cramer called on fans to "watch, enjoy and experience the moment."
The jewel in the crown of Dortmund's Westfalenstadion is the famous 'yellow wall', Europe's biggest standing terrace which holds 25,000 supporters.
"The emotion given by the yellow wall is so special that you need the people's attention. And if they just send messages and stream from the game, they lose this attention.
"And if we say Dortmund has this special atmosphere, then we have to keep going (with the project)."
Given the scheme's popularity -- Cramer said it has received "very, very positive feedback from our supporters" -- it will likely spread, although rivals Bayern are lukewarm.
Staying true to the inter-club rivalry between Germany's two biggest clubs, Bayern board member Rouven Kasper joked: "The football is so exciting at Bayern, we don't need to ban phones."
Cramer took the tongue-in-cheek jab in good nature and said the most important feedback was on the field, with Dortmund winning three from three since the scheme was implemented.
"(We did it) to win games -- and we did."

item.title: 'I thought he'd come back': Jesus on Ronaldo retirement
item.description:
Portugal coach Jorge Jesus said on Friday he had expected Cristiano Ronaldo to return to the national team despite their highly publicised rift, but respected the veteran forward's decision to retire from international football.
Ronaldo, 41, announced on Thursday that he would not play for Portugal again, bringing the curtain down on a record-breaking international career after a bitter end.
"Of course I thought he would come back, of course I thought I would call him up, of course I thought I would speak with him, but you have to respect him," Jesus told reporters after naming his squad for upcoming Nations League matches against Denmark and Wales.
"He decided that it was the moment to leave the national team."
Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to play a world record 234 times for his country, scoring 146 goals.
But his speed and edge have been blunted with age and he fell out with Jesus at the end of September.
The five-time Ballon d'Or winner accused the coach of broken promises after asking him to warm up during a match against Norway without bringing him on. Ronaldo immediately left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and token fine.
He apologised and it was rumoured he intended to return to the Portugal fold, but Ronaldo instead said that he had played his last match for his country.
"Sooner or later it had to happen. He felt it was the best moment to leave, and we have to respect that, while never forgetting what he represented for Portugal," said Jesus.
The 72-year-old coach, who previously managed Ronaldo at Saudi club Al-Nassr, said the interests of the national team had always been his top priority.
"All my decisions were made with the team in mind," said Jesus.
"I do not feel guilty in any way about his departure."
Portugal, who have already secured their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, host Denmark in Braga on November 14 before travelling to Wales three days later.
Jesus handed first call-ups to Monza striker Gustavo Varela, currently Serie A's leading scorer, and Porto right-back Alberto Costa, while Nuno Mendes and Francisco Conceicao miss out through injury.
Uncapped teenagers Rodrigo Mora and Geovany Quenda return to the squad, as does Club Brugge striker Carlos Forbs, who made his debut last year.
